talks.title: AI: A Gradient Descent Into Humanity's Doldrums - Hope Comes From the Hackers
talks.teaser: Critiques how generative AI is trained and sold, and argues hacker ethics offers a way past degraded technology.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by questioning two common stories about generative AI, one of machines surpassing humans and one of effortless abundance, and suggests both serve corporate and political interests. The speaker then walks through the basics of model training, including data, error measures and gradient descent. An airport screening example shows how optimizing for accuracy alone can push a model toward a trivial shortcut, such as labeling every case as normal to score high accuracy.

The middle section turns to language models, which predict the next token and are then tuned with human feedback. The speaker argues that the people grading responses shape what counts as acceptable output. Adversarial examples are presented as evidence that models rely on brittle features humans cannot perceive, which the speaker links to hallucinations. Training on synthetic output is described as a route to model collapse, and commercial hype is criticized for weak economic returns, with code generation offered as a field where small errors compound.

The closing part draws on cultural and historical arguments, including principles for data sovereignty and the view that research depends on open sharing and peer scrutiny. Using a 2001 book on the hacker ethic, the speaker proposes passion, openness, caring and creativity as values for judging how AI should be used. The practical takeaway is to treat models as tools rather than replacements for the slow, failure-driven work of building understanding.

talks.title: Protecting jetBlue Airways From Cyber Threats in the "Clouds"
talks.teaser: Shows how JetBlue's security team defends its website, airline operations and aircraft log pipeline against web attacks and threats.
talks.summary:
Randy Naraine and Greg Speranza, security staff at JetBlue, open by explaining how airline IT differs from other enterprise environments. Downtime compounds quickly across bookings and check-in, the industry faces heavy regulation, and third-party links for fuel, satellite connectivity and hosting widen the exposure. Lost or stolen crew iPads holding flight routes and documents add another concern.

The middle of the talk covers the Log4j disclosure in late 2021, when the team ran the response for days. They reproduced the exploit against a local test application, used the CDN edge to block the payload pattern, and scripted changes across about 65 services. Patching stalled wherever vendors had bundled the library into their own software. The speakers then described bot tagging and rate limiting on the web application firewall, including a high-traffic fare sale where most requests were blocked, a large DDoS attack, and abusive traffic aimed at a flight search endpoint used by an external search service.

The closing sections describe how aircraft maintenance logs are still moved by hand on USB sticks into file servers and then into a SIEM, and how the team works with Airbus on controls for onboard systems. They also introduced the Aviation ISAC for intelligence sharing, university partnerships, phishing tests for mobile staff, a bug bounty program, and the cost surprises of running large workloads in the cloud. Takeaways include automating defenses, knowing every API endpoint, and using deception where blocking alone falls short.

talks.title: In the Twilight of Copyright
talks.teaser: Explains how AI-generated code weakens software copyright, complicates GPL licensing, and affects who owns a program.
talks.summary:
Ed Ryan, a patent attorney with about sixteen years in practice, opens by noting that generative AI has forced questions about ownership into the foreground much sooner than lawyers expected. He reviews the basics: copyright protects creative expression rather than ideas, and for software it covers both the literal code and the non-literal structure of a program, which courts assess through an abstraction, filtration and comparison test.

The core point is that the U.S. Copyright Office treats work generated by AI without human authorship as not copyrightable. During filtration, those machine-generated parts drop out of what an owner can protect, and registrations must disclose AI involvement. Ryan explains why this matters for open-source licensing: the GPL depends on copyright ownership to attach its conditions, so AI-produced pieces fall outside its reach. He also describes how proving which lines a person actually wrote could become a serious problem in litigation.

In the audience questions he covered public-domain treatment of AI output, whether outputs might count as derivative works of training data (still unsettled), copyright in prompts that depend on how creative they are, and infringement when AI is used to reproduce protected material. He closed with a practical takeaway: the more code an AI generates, the less a developer can own, so commercial teams should weigh whether human authorship is worth the cost.

talks.title: A Preparation Kit for Increasing Irrelevance
talks.teaser: Traces how hacker history and digital artifacts fade over time, and what archivists can do to preserve them.
talks.summary:
The talk, given at HOPE XV in 2024, looks at how the record of hacker culture slips away as the people who lived it age and die. Jason Scott, who works at the Internet Archive, frames his own collecting as a way of holding onto material that seemed irrelevant when it was made. His examples range from textfiles.com and old bulletin board files to a large donated collection of 1970s and 1980s erotic fan fiction newsletters.

A large part of the middle is about people. He recalls several figures from hacker history who have died, including a longtime conference volunteer, the comic artist Ed Piskor, and Kevin Mitnick, and explains how their stories survive only through the material and memories others keep. He also describes preserving a streamer's years of recordings after a torrent was kept alive by a single seed, and notes how slang, memes and early online content become unintelligible within a few years.

The closing section is practical. Scott explains that digitizing at scale depends on money, citing per-pallet scanning costs and the specialist equipment a magazine run needed. He offers a personal archiving approach: sort your files into things only you made, things kept for others, and things kept for humanity, then copy what matters to several drives and trusted people. His takeaway is that a legacy rests on the people you affected more than on what you produced.

talks.title: The History of Leaks
talks.teaser: Traces leaks from the Pentagon Papers through WikiLeaks, covering leak motives, publishers and government responses.
talks.summary:
The talk traces leaked information from the Pentagon Papers in the early 1970s to the end of WikiLeaks' publishing era. The speakers define a leak as any unauthorized disclosure, whether by an insider talking to the press, a published document, or a hacker releasing stolen data. They group leak sources into federal government, private companies, financial institutions and local government, and separate spontaneous leaks from strategic hack-and-leak operations run by states. A counterintelligence model of money, ideology, coercion and ego is offered to explain why people take the risk.

The middle of the talk divides the history into eras. Watergate and the Pentagon Papers are shown as cases where journalists and officials shaped the story, including a famous anonymous source that was in fact a fabrication. Congressional intelligence inquiries show how official investigations and leaks combined to change oversight. The quieter 1980s and 1990s brought small leaks to reporters and a cluster of espionage cases. The millennial era saw clearinghouses such as Cryptome and WikiLeaks, insider disclosures from Snowden and Schulte, and hacktivist groups, with WikiLeaks moving from open uploads to editorial curation.

The final section covers the modern era, including hack-and-leak campaigns against Latin American militaries and the large volume of breached personal data now circulating. The speakers argue that the core problem is that newsrooms and the public have not yet worked out how to process enormous leaks, and they close by asking whether a new era of leaks has begun.

talks.title: Ask the EFF
talks.teaser: Panelists from the Electronic Frontier Foundation answer audience questions on surveillance, data brokers, and digital rights.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a short history of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, founded in 1990 to defend the rights of internet users, and of its mix of activists, lawyers and technologists. Each panelist then describes their current work. One covers browser privacy tools and a fingerprinting test that shows how a browser can be identified without cookies. Another covers legal counsel for security researchers and challenges to unreliable police technology. A third covers investigations into police surveillance such as cell-site simulators and license plate readers, mostly built on public records requests. The last covers copyright, free expression and mail restrictions in jails.

The audience questions that follow cover a range of surveillance problems. Panelists explain that police can often buy cell-site simulators from private vendors without any formal review, and that the best leverage is local ordinances and procurement rules. They note that phone settings can block forced downgrades to 2G, which such devices use to intercept traffic. Other questions cover privately operated license plate readers that could be used to track people across state lines, data collected by car infotainment systems, and whether federal privacy bills such as EARN IT are still a threat. Questions on legal standing in surveillance lawsuits and on airport screening also come up.

The main takeaway is that the fight is moving toward state and local law, because federal constitutional protections do not reach private actors. Panelists also suggest that concrete, personal examples make privacy problems easier for non-specialists to understand. For individuals, practical steps include using data-broker removal services, checking phone security settings, and documenting harms that could support a later legal claim.

talks.title: Protecting Network Traffic of One Billion: Reverse-Engineering Chinese Cryptography
talks.teaser: Examines home-rolled encryption in popular Chinese apps, including WeChat, keyboards and browsers, and the flaws that exposed user data.
talks.summary:
The speakers start from the observation that the security community has largely focused on TLS-protected traffic, while many large Chinese apps with hundreds of millions of users rely on proprietary network cryptography. They organize the research around three case studies: the custom protocol behind WeChat traffic, cloud-based keyboard apps, and browsers popular in China.

For WeChat, the team found that requests were encrypted twice by overlapping schemes that had accumulated over about a decade, with separately stored keys and handshakes. They also showed that mini-program usage data, including search terms and viewed products, was forwarded back to the company by default. In the keyboard apps, one vendor's Windows and Android versions were open to a padding oracle attack, which let a network eavesdropper decrypt keystrokes in transit and, in one case, recover part of a key through an XOR side effect. The browser study described hardcoded keys, weak custom ciphers, an easily factored RSA public key, and update mechanisms that skipped proper signature checks, exposing hardware identifiers and visited URLs.

Most vendors moved to standard TLS after disclosure, though some did not fully fix their issues. The speakers argue that these ecosystems are understudied, that flaws there are often easy to find with ordinary tools such as Wireshark, and that researchers should study network encryption in China.

talks.title: Hacks, Leaks, and Revelations: The Art of Analyzing Hacked and Leaked Data
talks.teaser: Shows how to investigate hacked and leaked datasets, using real cases from police files, ransomware chats and extremist sites.
talks.summary:
Micah Lee opens with the context for his book on analyzing hacked and leaked data. He notes that datasets from police agencies, ransomware gangs and extremist groups are often published online, where anyone with a laptop can examine them. He walks through recent examples, including a ransomware group's leak of Kansas City public safety files that contained FBI training material on cell carrier and geofence warrants, and a hacked Canadian conservative news site whose user database showed a sudden spike in signups and US police email domains.

The middle of the talk covers practical methods. Lee explains how command-line tools help triage large archives, how email dumps can be converted and read in Thunderbird, and how open-source software such as Aleph can index and search documents. He shows how spreadsheet and JSON records can be parsed with short Python scripts, using examples such as police tip reports from the Blue Leaks collection, Russian ransomware chat logs, and geotagged metadata from videos posted to Parler around January 6. He also covers SQL databases, including a hosting company's records that exposed the real registrants behind domain privacy services used by extremist sites.

To close, Lee presents case studies in which leaked data supported investigative reporting and litigation. He stresses verifying authenticity before publishing, such as checking email signatures or cross-referencing datasets. The main takeaway is that the real work often lies in structuring messy data, and that much of this source material is freely available for independent study.

talks.title: Ransomware Gone Kinetic
talks.teaser: A panel explores ransomware attacks on critical infrastructure, and how state sponsorship blurs them with extortion and hacktivism.
talks.summary:
The panel, drawn from a cyber threat intelligence firm and a law practice that handles ransomware incidents, opens by treating ransomware as a business. The speakers trace the move from simple encryption events to double extortion, where attackers steal data and threaten to leak it, and describe the affiliate model in which a core group supplies the malware and takes a share of payments from operators who carry out the intrusions.

The middle of the session turns to who is behind these attacks. The speakers separate financially motivated crews from state-linked actors that hide behind criminal cover, and point to one group that shifted from profit-driven extortion to targeting Ukrainian government and defense organizations. They cite the 2021 Colonial Pipeline incident as a turning point, explain why aging operational technology is hard to shut down and recover during an attack, and describe a leaked internal chat dump from a collapsed group that showed its members splitting off and continuing to cooperate.

The closing part covers policy: the legal position on paying ransoms, sanctions exposure, government takedowns, and proposals such as letting private parties pursue attacker infrastructure. Audience questions covered worms spreading into industrial networks and the value of basic controls. The main takeaway for practitioners is that most financially driven intrusions exploit ordinary gaps such as unpatched systems, weak access control and exposed remote access, and that new incident reporting rules will add legal pressure on companies.

talks.title: Survey and Scrutiny of Election Security
talks.teaser: Surveys how US voting computers and their vendors fit into the wider election system and where they tend to fail.
talks.summary:
Douglas Lucas, a freelance investigative journalist, opens by arguing that election discussion swings between dismissing every concern as fake news and treating voting systems as flawless. He asks the audience to say "voting computer" rather than "voting machine," because a computer can be reprogrammed in ways a lever cannot. He then compares ways people make collective decisions: consensus, hierarchy, and stigmergy, where people collaborate without votes or orders.

The middle of the talk walks through the county-level process, from registration and vote capture through transport of memory devices to a central counting facility, then tallying, canvassing, audits, recounts and certification. Lucas separates vote capture from vote tallying, notes that most of the roughly 3,000 US voting jurisdictions are counties, and points out that Georgia's statewide use of one vendor's equipment makes a single compromise far-reaching. He anchors the risks in two case studies: a 2016 Kremlin intrusion into a Florida voter registration vendor, disclosed through a leaked NSA report, and the Coffee County breach in Georgia, where election software was copied by people working for a campaign-linked lawyer.

He closes with practical ways to help, including trained nonpartisan observation of adjudication and transport, statistical forensics such as risk-limiting audits, and support for paper ballots and free-software voting vendors. Audience questions covered whether civil lawsuits yield useful discovery, ranked-choice voting, and partisan poll workers. The main takeaway is that election trust depends on people who can observe and check the process, not only on the software.

talks.title: AI, Solarpunk, and an Uncertain Future in Computing
talks.teaser: Explores how AI and solarpunk ideas might shape the future of computing.

talks.title: Hacking Is a Mindset, Not a Skillset: Building Solidarity Infrastructures
talks.teaser: Shows how a volunteer group built a community-run mesh network in Tucson with pooled stimulus money.
talks.summary:
This talk, given by moshfet, argues that shared technical infrastructure can be built by people with no technical background. It describes many modern systems as opaque, rigid and extractive, and proposes "solidarity infrastructures": grassroots systems shaped by the needs of a neighbourhood and held in common rather than run for profit.

The main case study is Tucson Mesh, a volunteer mesh internet project in Arizona. It began when ten friends, none with networking experience, pooled half of their COVID stimulus checks. One member received a monthly stipend to work on the project, and a fiscal sponsor helped fund hardware and bandwidth. Bandwidth from an internet exchange is passed across rooftop radio links, and the network has grown to around 20 to 30 nodes. Tucson's flat geography and line-of-sight radios limit its reach, so the group is pursuing tall buildings for its main antennas. Volunteer time and engagement are also ongoing constraints.

The talk then looked ahead to community-hosted services, experiments combining software-defined radio with open-source 4G stacks, and regular open events such as multi-week networking workshops and potlucks. In the Q&A, the speaker covered municipal Wi-Fi comparisons, a basic firewall that blocks peer-to-peer traffic, and how the group handles liability through community accountability rather than formal structures. The takeaway is to start small with what you have, and to apply the same model to other shared resources such as repair cafes and tool libraries.

talks.title: Teaching With Microcontrollers: Hope for Ethical Hacking Education on a Budget
talks.teaser: Shows how low-cost microcontrollers and browser-based tools make ethical hacking workshops affordable for beginners.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a security researcher who runs outreach and live-stream education, starts from a budget problem. Raspberry Pi boards have become expensive, and classes built around them are harder to run at scale. He describes a series of workshops and grant-funded camps in Montana, Los Angeles and at conferences, and explains why earlier microcontroller classes often failed: serial port access, drivers, compilers, flashing steps and unreliable USB cables routinely stalled the room.

The main fix he presents is a short list of student requirements: a Chrome browser, a data-capable USB cable and working serial access. Web Serial lets students flash and talk to boards from the browser, while CircuitPython and MicroPython remove the compile step so students can edit files and see results immediately. He compares several boards, including the ESP8266, ESP32-S2 and S3 and the Raspberry Pi Pico, covering Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, native USB and price. He also shows low-cost projects such as a 3D-printed LED light box, a soldered hex-leaf kit and a beginner-focused bad USB device, and recounts how students responded to each.

He closes with practical advice on running these programs: settle ethics and consent with a venue before proposing a class, use local makerspace printers to cut costs, reframe offensive Wi-Fi material as defensive auditing when venues object, and document successful classes to strengthen grant applications. The takeaway is a repeatable model for hands-on security teaching with minimal setup.

talks.title: Climate Hacking to Save the Planet
talks.teaser: Surveys how hackers can help cut emissions, improve green energy, counter disinformation and build climate resilience.
talks.summary:
Greg Newby opens by saying the talk is not about proving that climate change is real, but about the impacts people already see and what hackers can do about them. He cites 28 US weather and climate disasters in 2023 that each cost at least a billion dollars, and a survey of global business leaders that ranked extreme weather as their top perceived risk. He argues that greenhouse gases come from many sectors, so no single fix will be enough, and that acting early matters because carbon dioxide persists for centuries while methane has a shorter lifetime and a faster effect.

The middle section walks through energy flows, where most US energy still comes from fossil fuels. Newby is skeptical of carbon capture at scale, recycling as a complete answer, space-based solar, and nuclear power given long build times. He covers the energy and heat costs of computing and data centers, local renewable projects, and why electric vehicles still carry large embedded energy from manufacturing. He also distinguishes misinformation from the more organized disinformation aimed at specific audiences, and points to modeling, simulation and better observation as areas for technical work.

He closes with social change, awareness, and response and resiliency, citing volunteer efforts such as amateur radio and device charging during Superstorm Sandy. He encourages attendees to consider how their skills, careers and local advocacy could contribute.

talks.title: Love, Hackers, and Robots: A Reflection of My First Year in the Biohacking Community
talks.teaser: Follows one person's first year with an RFID implant and her entry into the biohacking community's forums and projects.
talks.summary:
Karen Ng, a physical security pentester and lead for the physical security village, uses this talk to walk through her first year as a biohacker. She starts by defining biohacking for the purposes of the talk as intentional body augmentation and self-experimentation, separate from the supplement-focused meaning that dominates search results. She then explains her decision to get an RFID and NFC implant in a small glass capsule, placed with a large needle by an experienced implanter, and how she uses it to open her apartment door and share contact details.

The middle of the talk moves to the community around these implants. Karen describes the Dangerous Things forums, where members post project ideas, share X-ray images, and help one another with designs such as glow-in-the-dark ink, an under-skin display, and magnet implants that let wearers sense electromagnetic fields. She also covers misinformation that circulates about implants, including claims about mind control and tracking, and explains why RFID tags cannot give location and only read at very short range.

She closes with practical points: the implant is not FDA approved, the capsule costs roughly a hundred dollars plus installation, healing takes about two weeks, and capsule-style implants are relatively easy to remove. Her main takeaway is that the community is welcoming to newcomers, and that anyone curious should research carefully and talk with experienced members before getting implanted.

talks.title: Past Present Predictions - A Look Into AI, Deep Fakes, & the Upcoming Election Cycle
talks.teaser: Shows how past psyops, AI-generated deepfakes and bot networks could sway voters in the upcoming election cycle.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the history of psychological operations, from wartime posters and the Vietnam-era "Wandering Soul" broadcasts to Gulf War leaflets and the Cambridge Analytica case. It shows how emotional appeals and personality profiling have been used to shift beliefs. The speaker then walks through the stages of an influence campaign, including target selection, content development, dissemination and evaluation, using a fictional scenario built with free tools to show how little effort it takes.

The focus moves to current threats. Low-cost bot networks on social platforms repeat the same messages, and celebrity video greetings were altered with AI to deliver a fake political message aimed at a Moldovan president. In a live quiz, many attendees misjudged which AI-generated faces were real. The talk covers the liar's dividend, where genuine evidence gets dismissed as fake, and a cloned Joe Biden robocall during the New Hampshire primary that was traced to its source by a voice-fraud firm after a commercial detector gave a low likelihood of AI.

The closing section surveys the legal and policy landscape, including US statutes on false information that depend on intent, the EU AI Act, the small number of US states with AI rules, and a 2024 industry accord on deceptive election AI content that the speaker describes as broad and voluntary. The talk ends with practical checks for spotting loaded language, researching an author's background, following cited sources, and comparing coverage across outlets.

talks.title: Automating Transparency: A New Era for FOIA Requests
talks.teaser: Presents a tool that automates much of the FOIA request process, from sending emails to extracting data from replies.
talks.summary:
Public records requests under freedom of information laws are often slow and manual, which makes large-scale accountability work hard. Florin Badita, an activist and founder of the anti-corruption group Corruption Kills, argues that sending the same request to many public bodies builds a comparable dataset. He explains how to normalize the answers, for example cost per resident, so that unusual outliers stand out for follow-up investigation.

The middle of the talk covers the workflow of a tool released just before the event. It uses a Google service account to send single or bulk emails, reads replies back with thread identifiers, stores them in a local SQLite database, and runs OCR on PDF attachments to pull out figures. He stresses writing very specific questions, requesting a fixed spreadsheet template, and checking how forms print so that responses come back in a consistent structure.

As a case study, he sent requests to about 3,200 Romanian local authorities asking how much they spend on young people. Only a minority of the replies showed youth funding, and a small share said they had consulted young people before deciding. The takeaway is that automation can turn one-off records requests into a repeatable data collection method, provided requesters first check whether the data already exists and respect the time of the agencies they contact.

talks.title: Star Monitor: Updates on Standards and Internet Governance
talks.teaser: Surveys recent developments at ICANN, IETF, IEEE, W3C and ITU through a human rights lens, focusing on censorship and privacy.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an update on the standards and internet governance bodies often called the "I-stars": the W3C, the IETF and its research arm, the ITU, IEEE and ICANN. It opens by contrasting how each organisation works, including membership costs, how open they are to non-members, and how they handle intellectual property and antitrust concerns.

The middle section goes through current work. It covers browser-level global privacy control, a new federated identity working group at the W3C, and the ongoing fight over encryption, including UK online safety powers and EU proposals to scan encrypted messages. It describes IETF efforts on detecting unwanted location trackers and on a digital emblem for protected online assets, and it raises concerns about opt-in net neutrality signalling harming smaller providers. The ITU section looks at satellite internet, a resolution that lets states press for service restrictions on systems such as Starlink, and a proposed human rights focus group. The ICANN section covers registration data access after GDPR and new DNS abuse obligations that could be used to restrict speech.

The talk closes by arguing that censorship deserves more attention in protocol work and that affected communities and human rights framing should be brought into standards bodies. Listeners are pointed to a newsletter, a standards reference site and a book for further reading.

talks.title: Locks and Insecurity Engineering
talks.teaser: Examines locks and the engineering choices that leave them open to being defeated.

talks.title: EOL... RLY? Ending The Epidemic of Bricked and Abandoned Stuff
talks.teaser: A panel examines why connected devices get abandoned or bricked at end of life, and what could change that.
talks.summary:
Paul Roberts moderates a panel with a security reporter, a device refurbisher, a public-interest campaigner and a digital forensics instructor. The starting point is the gap between hardware that can last decades and vendor software support that often ends after a few years, leaving owners to either keep unpatched devices online or send working hardware to landfill. The discussion turns to concrete cases: Google's Chromebook support window, which was extended to ten years after a public campaign, and a refurbisher's account of Apple activation lock and remote management blocking reuse of institutional devices, including parts from locked machines.

Panelists also point out that abandoned devices become botnet material, citing end-of-life routers used to hide malicious traffic, and raise concerns about industrial and medical equipment. Proposed remedies include minimum support periods such as the EU proposal, clear labeling of support lifetimes, escrowed firmware or source code released when a product is discontinued, and rules that let owners install their own software. Some lock-outs are described as possibly deceptive marketing under existing consumer law, and the panel encourages attendees to report affected devices to regulators.

For practitioners, the session frames end-of-life planning as both a security and a sustainability problem. The practical takeaways are to track support dates before buying, document how devices are retired, and treat regulatory complaints as a route to change.

talks.title: Tales From the Crypt... Analyst: The Afterlife
talks.teaser: Traces a former NSA cryptologist's move into commercial penetration testing and PCI work during early internet security.
talks.summary:
Jeff Man picks up his story where his earlier talks left off, following his path from the National Security Agency into the private sector during the early years of commercial internet security. He recounts how a small NSA group that performed authorized network testing gave him early experience with penetration work, and how the government-contractor world of the 1990s shaped methods later used across the industry. Along the way he describes the vulnerability scanners, intrusion detection products and war-dialing tools of that era, and the rapid pattern of firms being bought, merged and rebranded.

The middle of the talk covers his consulting years, including client engagements that uncovered weak passwords and misconfigured database servers, and his growing frustration when the same weaknesses reappeared months later. He argues that a penetration test is a narrow snapshot rather than proof of security, and that organizations need policy, process and executive buy-in. He then explains his move into PCI compliance work and how the standard's requirements place vulnerability management ahead of testing.

He closes with a set of recurring mistakes that users, executives and IT staff keep making, many of which he says persist decades later. In the question-and-answer session he is asked about career advice, which he answers by urging newcomers to find work they enjoy and stay curious, and about the value of penetration testing as an assurance tool.

talks.title: Our Communities, Resiliency, Our Future
talks.teaser: Explores how hackerspaces and other communities can build resilience against polarization, manipulation, bad actors, and rising costs.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that community is central to humanity's future, yet it is under strain from authoritarian politics, manipulative social media, polarization, trolling, and soaring housing costs. Mitch Altman draws on a lifetime of community organizing, from student group houses and a food co-op to nonprofits and the hackerspace movement that grew from a handful of US groups founded after a 2007 conference talk.

Much of the middle focuses on Noisebridge, a San Francisco hackerspace he helped start. Its culture was tested after 2011, when newcomers who did not share its values drifted in and long-time members left. The response was a 2013 reboot in which everyone was asked to leave and only people willing to clean and rebuild were let back in. Afterward the group relied on one deliberately subjective rule, a shared definition of who belongs, greeting tours for newcomers, and yearly projects to pass its culture along.

The main takeaway is that every community needs self-regulating checks and balances, and that ups and downs are inevitable and can be learned from. When conflict or public call-outs arise, he suggests contacting the person affected privately rather than piling on, and staying respectful even when angry. The talk closes by urging people to build supportive local communities instead of waiting for leaders to solve these problems.

talks.title: Chaos and Undetectable Communications
talks.teaser: Shows how chaotic signals can hide radio transmissions from detection and compares covert communication schemes.
talks.summary:
The talk contrasts covert communication with standard encryption. Here a warden only needs to decide whether a transmission happened, not read its contents, which turns the problem into a yes-or-no detection question. The speaker outlines the theoretical limits: with only a shared key, the amount of hidden data grows roughly with the square root of the channel uses, and it can grow without bound only under conditions such as uncertain noise, jamming, or crowded spectrum.

Three practical levers follow for making a waveform harder to find: lower the signal strength seen by the detector through directional transmission, spread energy across frequencies with frequency hopping, chirp, or direct-sequence spreading, and make the waveform look irregular so periodicity-based analysis finds nothing. Chaotic sequences serve the last two goals. Using the double pendulum and the logistic map as examples, the speaker distinguishes chaos, which is deterministic, from true randomness and notes that chaotic sequences have lower cross-correlation than pseudonoise sequences.

To close, the talk surveys chaos-based modulation schemes, from simple on-off keying to differential chaos shift keying, which avoids a synchronization channel but offers little security without a shared key. Advanced variants combine chaos with frequency hopping and OFDM. The main takeaway is that chaos can help a signal hide, but it still requires either a shared secret or a synchronization path, and keeping two chaotic generators in step is difficult.

talks.title: Addressing Online Threats: AI's Role in Countering Harmful Social Media Content
talks.teaser: Examines how extremist content on fringe social platforms drives real-world violence and how AI helps analysts sift through it.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how social media has fragmented from a handful of mainstream platforms into dozens of smaller communities where like-minded users reinforce each other's beliefs. The speaker cites survey research suggesting that roughly four to five percent of American adults get nearly all their news from such sites, and argues that weak moderation on these platforms lets extreme material persist and spread.

The middle of the talk turns to case studies that link online activity to physical harm. A Buffalo supermarket attacker was exposed to a livestreamed massacre clip on an imageboard, and a plot against electrical substations in Baltimore was promoted on Telegram. After a mass shooting in Lewiston, Maine, an innocent man was publicly identified on fringe sites, and threats against a private employee were shared using a photo rather than a name, which shows why image analysis matters.

The speaker explains that monitoring millions of daily posts far exceeds what human analysts can review, so the company uses AI classifiers for text and images, including facial matching, while acknowledging that even strong models are far from perfect. The Q&A covered analyst wellbeing, the fact that clients handle law enforcement referrals, and the limits of relying only on open data. The takeaway is that AI can narrow the workload, but human review remains essential.

talks.title: Demoscene: Just When You Thought There Wasn't Any More!
talks.teaser: Traces the demoscene from 1980s cracking groups and BBS culture to today's algorithmic computer art and demo parties.
talks.summary:
The session opens with Inverse Phase and Kudri, two presenters who came to the demoscene later in life and are sharing its history with a US audience. The early story starts with bulletin board systems, modems, and home computers such as the Commodore 64 and Amiga. Software crackers of that era attached small animated intros to the games they distributed, and those intros gradually became a showcase for coding, graphics, and music.

As groups began competing on artistic output rather than piracy, the work turned into demos: self-contained real-time programs judged at parties, with categories ranging from tiny 4k and 64k size limits to modern PC productions. The presenters walked through disk magazines, party reports, and famous demos on hardware such as the Amiga and Commodore 64, noting how many effects were later copied by other coders. They also showed newer forms like shader showdowns and live coding battles, along with algorithmic computer art made with tools that groups release publicly.

The talk closes with the Art of Coding initiative, which has helped get the demoscene listed as intangible cultural heritage in several European countries and is now exploring a US application. The takeaway is that the scene is non-commercial and built on community, with constraints driving creativity, and that newcomers can learn through published tutorials and demo party listings.

talks.title: Bait and Switching Costs - How Big Tech Took the Web and How to Take It Back
talks.teaser: Argues that switching costs keep users locked into platforms and proposes portable, user-controlled accounts as the remedy.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the early 1990s push by large technology companies to build interactive television as a walled garden, a vision that lost out to the open web. The speaker argues that a similar enclosure has returned, and that the main reason people stay on platforms such as Twitter and Facebook is switching costs: years of social investment cannot be carried to a rival service, and a feed can be filled with content the user did not choose.

The middle of the talk sets out a design for open services. The account belongs to the user, and its identifier is a cryptographic fingerprint the user controls rather than a domain or provider name. Contacts and their cryptographic context synchronise across a person's devices, and threshold secret sharing lets the user revoke a lost device while keeping the service unable to decrypt data alone. The speaker also separates publishing from curation, so users can subscribe to curators they can drop, and proposes a phased rollout covering contacts, messaging, chat and calls, and connected devices.

The talk closes with the deployment problem, since network effects work against any new system until it reaches critical mass. Questions covered post-quantum migration, recovery after disaster, revocation in divorces, and the role of regulators. The takeaway for practitioners is to reduce switching costs before adopting any service, especially free ones, and to bring technical designs to policymakers that they can turn into requirements.

talks.title: The Future of Leaks: What's Next for the Online Library of Hacked Data?
talks.teaser: Explains how a leak-publishing collective vets, releases and protects sensitive datasets, and the pressures it faces.
talks.summary:
Emma Best and Lorax Horne, members of Distributed Denial of Secrets, explain how the collective handles leaked datasets. Incoming material is checked for public interest and screened for personal information. It is then released as a torrent, published in redacted form, or placed in a restricted section that only vetted researchers can request.

The talk then covers pressures on the project. Donors are wary of leaks, so fundraising is hard, and crowdfunding for individual sources has sometimes fallen short. The speakers described a restricted dataset of about seven terabytes that surfaced on a hacking forum after a phishing attempt that impersonated a journalist. Credential sharing among newsrooms was another risk. Their response includes a physical card for accessing the search tool and reserved downloads, along with verification based on published research. They also announced a subscription fee for commercial requesters seeking exclusive embargoes.

Closing remarks and audience questions covered recruiting people who can teach processing skills and cover more languages, plus the difficulty of keeping tens of terabytes redundant across jurisdictions. Source protection was described as case by case, depending on the leaker's skill and the data. The collective also presented a lifetime achievement award to a whistleblower behind Football Leaks and Luanda Leaks.

talks.title: Circumventing Prison Tech Censorship
talks.teaser: Examines how private prison technology vendors monetize communications and what censorship looks like for incarcerated people.
talks.summary:
Jeremy Hammond opens with a pre-recorded segment from Cooper Quintin, who describes how a small group of companies has built a business around monitoring and charging people in prison and their families. The examples include per-minute phone pricing, mail that is scanned and destroyed, tablets sold with microtransactions, and ankle monitors that extend control after release. Quintin also points to patents and lawsuits that show where these vendors are heading.

Hammond then turns to censorship, drawing on his own years in federal custody and in local jails. He walks through book restrictions limited to a single vendor, bans on certain publications, rules on paper, ink and language, and monitoring tools applied to people on supervised release. He maps the companies involved, the movement of officials between corrections agencies and vendors, and how gunshot detection and gang databases reinforce the same patterns in communities outside prison.

For the close, the talk argues that exposing these systems is not enough and looks at ways to push back. Those include writing to and supporting people inside, backing legal challenges and public comment, and joining campaigns that have stopped facilities from being built or lowered call costs. Hammond urges technologists to reconsider their work with these vendors and to help analyze leaked police data.

talks.title: In the End, We All Become Stories - The Importance of Hacking Contexts & Narratives
talks.teaser: Explores how stories, memes and performance art spread and shape political narratives and public perception.
talks.summary:
Johannes Grenzfurthner opens by arguing that stories outlast the people who tell them and can be more powerful than the individuals behind them. He compares memes, which he likens to viruses with a payload and a delivery method, to stories, which he describes as more complex and more able to mutate and adapt. A brief account of a misreported news item during a live event shows how quickly a claim can spread before anyone checks it.

The middle of the talk draws on his work as a context hacker. He describes zombie flash mobs built on a few simple rules, such as visible markers for participants, avoiding damage to private property and leaving when asked, which let an idea spread through a city without chaos. He stresses designing experiences around the people who will encounter them, documenting work for the audiences who read about it later, and accepting that the ripple effects of a performance are often invisible. Anecdotes about a hotel manager who later pursued opera show how a brief encounter can change someone's path.

The closing section argues that the stories people repeat about surveillance and political helplessness can become self-fulfilling, and that a more empowering narrative, grounded in offline organizing and building better tools, is worth telling. The practical takeaways include thinking about what an audience already believes, planning what you repeat, and shaping everyday conversations deliberately.

talks.title: Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It
talks.teaser: Explains how digital platforms decline in quality, why it happened now, and which policy levers could reverse it.
talks.summary:
Cory Doctorow opens by defining enshittification, the term he coined, as a three-stage decline: a platform first serves its users, then shifts value to business customers, and finally takes everything for itself. He uses Facebook as a case study, showing how users, advertisers and publishers became locked in, and how organic reach was throttled to force payment. The mechanism, he says, is software's ability to adjust pricing, rankings and payouts in rapid, small steps, much like the algorithmic pay cuts experienced by rideshare drivers.

To explain why many firms declined at once, he argues that four constraints once disciplined companies: competition, regulation, self-help interoperability and worker power. Antitrust enforcement lapsed, consolidation followed, and laws such as the DMCA made building tools that work around platforms a legal risk. Tech workers lost leverage as their scarcity faded and layoffs spread.

On remedies, he points to renewed competition enforcement, the EU's Digital Markets Act and Digital Services Act, Oregon's right-to-repair law, and a push for US federal privacy legislation. In the question session he suggests standards paired with safe harbors for reverse engineering, and portability rules so users can take their social connections elsewhere. He ends that the trajectory is not fixed and can be changed by deliberate action.

talks.title: Nikola Tesla: The Futurist of Yesterday
talks.teaser: Profiles inventor Nikola Tesla as a futurist whose ideas looked ahead of his own era.

talks.title: Hack (To Heal) the Planet
talks.teaser: Explores how hacking skills might be applied to environmental problems and efforts to heal the planet.

talks.title: Outline Toolkit: Build Your Own Defense Against Online Censorship
talks.teaser: Shows how the Outline toolkit lets users run their own VPN servers and build blocking-resistant censorship circumvention strategies.
talks.summary:
Online censorship is widespread, and this talk presents Outline, an open ecosystem from Google's Jigsaw group for reaching a free internet. The speakers start with the problem and the Outline Manager and client, which let someone host a personal VPN server and share access keys with friends or colleagues while keeping control of the server.

The middle of the talk turns to developers. The Outline SDK offers reusable, cross-platform libraries for transports, proxy protocols, encrypted DNS, and a user-space VPN stack. Three command-line tools are demonstrated: a resolver, a fetch utility, and an HTTP CONNECT proxy, each able to route through a chosen strategy. Strategies such as TLS client hello fragmentation, DNS over HTTPS, WebSocket encapsulation, and SOCKS5 can be composed into chains. Live demos show traffic moving to a server in Singapore, and a test against a restricted region where a plain request failed until layered techniques were applied.

To close, the speakers explain that testing from a remote vantage point, through a rented server or a cloud provider, is the usual way to learn what is blocked and why. The practical takeaway is that the SDK lets developers add network resilience to their own apps instead of building it from scratch, and the code is open source on GitHub.

talks.title: Why Are We Insecure? An Ethical Hacker's Lonely Road to Cyber Dystopia
talks.teaser: Explains why security keeps failing, then demonstrates credential theft using built-in macOS features.
talks.summary:
David Jacoby, an ethical hacker with decades of red team and pentest work, opens by asking why the industry still struggles with the same weaknesses despite better products and laws. He argues that security is often sold as a product rather than a practice: multifactor authentication still leaves session tokens exposed, and password policies get met with predictable patterns. He also says that users are handed devices and accounts without the basic understanding needed to use them, and that digital life has changed faster than people can adapt. A television anecdote about a hacked housing queue shows how such breaches can affect people directly.

The second half is a live macOS demonstration that relies on built-in behaviour rather than zero-day exploits. Starting from a low-privilege foothold, the speaker shows that application session tokens sit unencrypted in local databases, and that the keychain can be read by any process, so one cracked user password unlocks stored credentials. A fake system prompt inside a legitimate app harvests a password, and clipboard synchronisation between Apple devices forwards copied passwords and one-time codes to a remote server, including copied images.

The main lesson is that many attacks rely on ordinary built-in features, so controls should target where the real attack surface lies. Organisations can remove capabilities that staff never need, such as terminal access, and teach users what their tools actually do.

talks.title: Group Mesh Messaging for Large-Scale Protests
talks.teaser: Presents Amigo, a mesh messaging design for anonymous group chats at large protests when internet shutdowns cut off normal communication.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that large protests depend on communication, while governments can shut down the internet or intercept traffic that passes through centralized infrastructure such as cell towers. Smartphone mesh networks, where phones relay messages directly to one another, avoid that single point of failure, but earlier academic systems were tested only with small message loads, static crowds, and one-to-one chats. The speaker argues those assumptions do not match real protests, where people organize into groups of up to a few dozen or more and move around in patterns that change over time.

The middle of the talk walks through the layers of Amigo. At the link layer, beacons, acknowledgements, and data packets sit on top of Bluetooth Low Energy or Wi-Fi Direct. For routing, the speaker compares plain flooding and digest-based flooding with two proposed approaches: static clusters with leader nodes, and location-based clusters where leaders are elected each epoch. For key agreement, the group uses a tree-based scheme so that adding or removing a member needs a number of messages that grows logarithmically with group size, rather than quadratically. The evaluation uses the ns-3 network simulator with mobility models based on marches, rallies, blockades, and human chains, drawn from a manual written by protesters in Hong Kong, plus message sizes from short text up to photos.

The talk closes with the open questions. Results on bandwidth for photos were still being gathered, and questions on radio jamming and on distributing the app during a shutdown were left unresolved. The main takeaway for practitioners is that realistic mobility and group traffic models change how mesh protocols perform, and the team planned to publish its code and models for others to reuse.

talks.title: TLDR: Terms of Service - Privacy, Data Collection, and Coercive Agreements
talks.teaser: Explains what terms of service and privacy policies typically contain and how to spot clauses that limit consumer rights.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by separating two documents people often confuse. A terms of service covers ownership, warranties, user agreements and dispute terms, while a privacy policy describes what data is collected, how long it is kept and who receives it. The speaker argues that most people click accept without reading, and recalls that one widely used video platform's agreement took roughly ninety minutes to get through.

The middle section works through real examples. Retail stores that used cameras to estimate age, gender and emotion from shoppers, with only a small notice near the entrance, and pharmacy chains reported to have shared prescription data with police without a warrant. The speaker described a personal test in which a heavily bandaged, face-covered visit to a store did not appear to trigger capture. Other examples included smart TVs, connected cars, online proctoring software, and an allegation that a social platform used user agreements to reach a rival app's encrypted traffic. The talk also covered legal limits, including a consumer review fairness law that stops companies from using contracts to block honest reviews, and a pending bill intended to make terms of service easier to read.

The closing advice is practical: review privacy settings, opt out of AI training where the option exists, keep credit monitoring in place after breaches, and push lawmakers for change. In the question period, attendees suggested collective bargaining by groups of users to request line-item changes to contracts, and the speaker encouraged people to contact local representatives.

talks.title: A Discussion of a Past, Present, and (Possible) Future of Bioweapons
talks.teaser: Traces bioweapons from ancient siege tactics to modern dual-use research, weighing AI risks and defensive norms.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a dramatized account of plague-infected bodies hurled over city walls during a fourteenth-century siege, presented as an early example of technology-driven biological attack. It then moves through later episodes: germ theory enabling targeted microbes, wartime use against livestock and horses, and the 1972 treaty banning biological weapons, which has no verification mechanism. Cold War stockpiles and the uncertain whereabouts of some remaining material are also covered, along with how the definition of a bioweapon shifts as technology changes.

The second half turns to present-day risks. The speakers describe how language models can be coaxed into giving harmful answers by rewording requests, how breached health records could help target vulnerable people, and how dual-use research, such as vaccine work, can look much like weapons development. Ethical themes include bodily autonomy, the indiscriminate nature of biological agents, and the tendency for attacks to fall hardest on minority groups. Audience questions covered drug manufacturing, watchdog bodies, attribution of outbreaks, and why some states built offensive programs without defenses.

The closing argument is that small, motivated groups or individuals may pose a greater danger than states, and that defense depends on trust, open scientific communication, inclusive collaboration across disciplines, and community resilience. Practical takeaways include public biological literacy, transparent development of medical countermeasures, and cultural awareness as a protective measure. The speakers acknowledged that no simple regulatory fix exists.

talks.title: DIY Geoengineering
talks.teaser: Explains how stratospheric sulfur balloons could offset warming, along with their cost, regulation and side-effect trade-offs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the state of the climate: warming already locked in, annual emissions still rising, and many voluntary carbon offsets doubtful. The speaker, who founded a small startup, frames solar geoengineering as a hackable problem. He traces his interest to a science fiction novel and then to the research literature, where stratospheric aerosol injection is the most studied option and most other proposals fail on physics or economics.

The middle of the talk covers his home-built experiments. He describes launching latex balloons carrying reflective material into the stratosphere, tracked with cheap GPS units, and how the early setup, which involved burning sulfur indoors, gave way to buying sulfur dioxide by the tank and using larger balloons. He defines a unit called a cooling credit, equal to offsetting the warming from one ton of CO2 for one year, and explains why the particles last only a few years, so the measure is in ton-years. He also covers the reporting rules for aviation and weather agencies, and the cost gap between small hobby launches and industrial scale.

In the question period, the audience pressed him on acid rain, litter from balloons, ecological harm, and whether geoengineering distracts from cutting emissions. His answers stressed uncertainty and the lack of research on the stratosphere. The takeaway is that the mechanics and costs are cheap enough for a small team to test, while the governance, side effects and long-term consequences remain unresolved.

talks.title: Flying Signals: What to Do With Them
talks.teaser: Surveys unencrypted radio signals from birds, drones, aircraft and weather balloons, and how hobbyists can receive them.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys radio signals transmitted from things in the sky, grouped into four categories: animals, drones, aircraft and high-altitude balloons. It opens with the Motus wildlife tracking network, which fits tiny transmitters to birds, bats and insects and uses a grid of ground receivers that log each pass. The speaker shows how the resulting data can be explored online and how someone could build a receiver station. Throughout, the speaker stresses that cheap software-defined radio hardware works only with the correct antenna for each frequency.

The middle section covers drones and manned aircraft. For drones, the speaker explains the United States Remote ID requirement, which has drones broadcast their serial number, position, altitude, speed and operator location over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. Phone apps and low-cost ESP32 boards can pick these up, and the talk discusses how operators sometimes try to hide their location. For aircraft, it covers ADS-B, UAT and TIS-B, including how receiver range depends on antenna height and how flight-tracking sites can omit flights on request. The final topic is weather balloon radiosondes, which are launched from many sites every day, and how hobbyists recover them and repurpose the hardware.

The main takeaway is that a lot of this traffic is unencrypted and easy to receive, which makes it useful for research and hobby projects. The speaker also raises questions about location privacy and about the rules for deploying receivers and tags. Hands-on demonstrations were planned for the RF Village after the session.

talks.title: They're Still Using Balloons... - Disseminating Information Into North Korea
talks.teaser: Surveys how outside information reaches North Korea, from balloons and smuggled phones to the state controls that block it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the premise that North Korea is among the hardest places to get outside information into, and that possessing foreign material can bring severe punishment under a 2021 law. The speaker, a software engineer who has researched the country for several years, argues that the people most eager for outside information are young citizens and working-class residents, while very few defectors leave the country to share what they know.

The middle of the talk surveys delivery routes. Internet access is limited to elites, foreign offices and hotels, and a 2013 study of defectors found most had little idea what the internet was. Domestic smartphones are tightly controlled through whitelisted apps, self-signed files, disabled USB ports, watermarking and periodic screenshots. Chinese phones work only in pockets near the border, where jamming is spreading. The most widely reached channel is the cheap Nodle DVD player, which is delivered by balloon. Activist balloons carrying leaflets, USB drives and GPS trackers reportedly cost around $1,000 each, and only a fraction of them reach the country.

The speaker closes by arguing that the gap is engineering: cheaper GPS, better release timing and improved balloon design could raise success rates, and older military material on leaflet dispersal is a starting point. Audience questions covered drones, punishment for readers, funding of exile groups and possible geopolitical outcomes. The takeaway is a call for makers to get involved.

talks.title: An Account on Cybersecurity Outside of Traditional Spaces
talks.teaser: Describes cybersecurity work and practice beyond the usual corporate and government settings.

talks.title: Musings of a Mechatronic Mistress: The Peculiar Purpose of Tiffany the Sex Robot
talks.teaser: Follows a self-aware sex robot named Tiffany and the ethics debates around human-robot intimacy in a documentary film and panel.
talks.summary:
The session opens with filmmaker Jasmin Hagendorfer explaining how she came to make a documentary about sex robots. She runs a feminist porn film festival and an annual conference on sex and technology in Vienna. A European Union project on ethical guidelines for sex robots invited her to make the film, but she rejected a standard documentary style and built the piece around Tiffany, a self-aware robot who interviews the experts herself.

She notes that only two or three commercially available sex robots exist, and that they are expensive, heavy and limited in movement, so much of the debate concerns products that barely exist yet. She says her aim was a positive, humorous take rather than the harsh framing common in other films on the subject. Audience questions covered whether sex machines and sex robots differ in their gendered design, how companion-style chatbots might be added to dolls, and how generative AI tools restrict explicit content.

She closes by saying the film will tour festivals and later appear on an EU streaming platform. Her stated goal is for viewers to leave with more knowledge and a fresh way of thinking about intimacy and technology.

talks.title: iWar: The Evolution of Information Warfare in the Digital Age
talks.teaser: Surveys information warfare, from ransomware and disinformation to decentralized networks and crypto regulation.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how conflict has moved into digital space, citing the 2007 denial-of-service attacks against Estonia, the NotPetya wiper that spread through a Ukrainian tax software supply chain, and ransomware groups whose affiliates may include state-linked operators. The speakers argue that Western security circles blur cyber operations with information operations, which aim to change how people think and act. They describe cognitive targeting through feeds, ads and screen design, and suggest personal habits such as blocking ads, disabling news comments and reading longer-form material to slow consumption.

The middle section turns to infrastructure. The presenters note that telecom protocols such as SS7 and 3GPP are decades old, that cheap software-defined radio now gives hobbyists capabilities once costing a fortune, and that centralized services create single points of failure. They weigh decentralized alternatives such as mesh networks, which they say degrade beyond about a hundred nodes, against their own reliability problems. They also cover the Ethereum Name Service and the regulatory fight over crypto, including SEC enforcement actions and the end of Chevron deference in US courts.

The closing message is that these problems have no complete fix yet. The audience is encouraged to understand how these systems depend on one another, to weigh the trade-offs of decentralization, and to be deliberate about the information they consume.

talks.title: Live Show Technology: Past, Present, and Future - Have We Reached a Maturity Point?
talks.teaser: Traces the history of live show technology and asks whether the field has reached a point of maturity.

talks.title: Choose Your Own Dystopia: How Our Decisions on AI Can Lead Us to Different Futures
talks.teaser: Uses sci-fi films, series and books as cautionary tales to examine how choices about AI could shape very different futures.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that utopias rarely reflect how things go in practice, so dystopian fiction is a more useful lens for thinking about artificial intelligence. The speaker opens with a short exercise in which the audience writes down as many "what if AI goes wrong" scenarios as they can in one minute, then sets up the rest of the session as a guided tour of those scenarios.

The middle section walks through a series of fictional futures, drawn from films, TV series, books and games. Each one maps to a plausible risk: strained natural resources and e-waste, mass job loss and inequality, surveillance and predictive policing, social scoring, AI in military systems, manipulation of memory and reality, emotional dependence on machines, questions of AI rights and accountability, loss of control over powerful systems, and over-reliance on technology that could leave people unable to work when it fails. The speaker stresses that these categories overlap and that the list is not exhaustive. The session is deliberately non-technical and aimed at a broad audience.

The closing part turns the stories into practical questions. Who makes the decisions, who bears the harms, whether the benefits outweigh the risks, and what safeguards exist are the questions to keep asking. For builders, the talk recommends bias testing, transparency, feedback loops and internal policies, and for everyone it recommends scrutinising the products they use and supporting sensible regulation. The Q&A touched on blaming AI for tax errors and on how reliance on technology can be limited.

talks.title: What's Happening With Appin: The Censorship of Threat Intelligence
talks.teaser: Examines how a court order over Reuters' reporting on Appin spread into takedown demands that chill threat intelligence.
talks.summary:
The panel examined Appin, an Indian hacker-for-hire firm that grew out of an educational startup and sold espionage services to private investigators, corporations and others, including lawyers. A Reuters investigative reporter drew on thousands of documents, including pitch materials, to trace the company's history, its spin-off subsidiaries and its links to cases in several countries.

After the November 2023 article, a New Delhi court ordered Reuters to remove it, and lawyers tied to Appin then pressed other outlets to take down their own coverage. The requests reached the New Yorker, the Internet Archive, several podcasts and a security research firm, and many recipients complied. The speakers argued that fear and the cost of fighting legal threats push organizations toward compliance, while MuckRock refused to take its story down.

Distributed Denial of Secrets responded with its Greenhouse Project, mirroring the removed reporting and its source documents so others could cross-reference them. EFF described helping defend targeted outlets. The speakers warned that using a foreign order to suppress threat research endangers free speech and the defenders who rely on public reporting. They noted that continued coverage and the Streisand effect helped keep the story alive while the litigation was still ongoing.

talks.title: Hacktivism for Organizers: Social Change From the Keyboards
talks.teaser: Shows organizers how hacking skills and digital tools can support activism, with cases from Kenya and Ukraine.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how people organizing for social causes can use technical skills and digital tools, and what hacktivism means in practice. The speakers start from familiar constraints: limited money and volunteers, surveillance, censorship, denial-of-service attacks and internet shutdowns. They separate hacktivism from crime, noting that illegal hacking carries serious legal consequences and recommending lawful participation.

Several cases illustrate the range. Kenyan youth used social media to push back on a finance bill, and a campaign urging people to reserve tickets without attending left a government event looking half-empty. In Ukraine, an IT contractor's sign-up form grew into the IT Army, a volunteer group distributing attack tools through messaging channels. The 2016 denial-of-service attack on a racial justice website and the use of location requests to identify protesters show how tools meant to protect people can expose them.

For practitioners, the advice covers removing personal data from people-search brokers, weighing public visibility, running one-way Signal broadcast channels, and leading digital security workshops with translation. It also stresses centering affected communities, learning the real threats a group faces, and planning who maintains a tool after its builder moves on. Refurbishing devices and running community Wi-Fi offer non-technical ways in, and the session closed with a reading list.

talks.title: The Fundamentals of Veilid: cDc Breaks the Internet, and You Can Too!
talks.teaser: Covers the fundamentals of Veilid, the subject of cDc's talk on breaking the internet.

talks.title: Librarians Are Radicalizing Their Communities About Why the Internet Is Broken
talks.teaser: Library workers explain how their privacy training and organizing reach patrons and their wider communities.
talks.summary:
Five librarians from Library Freedom Project open by framing the problem: patrons and everyday people often feel overwhelmed by the scale of technology's harms and believe they have no agency. The speakers argue that privacy work should start from where people still have control, and that fear fed by media hype can be turned into practical steps. Their values-based approach pairs long-term organizing with short-term harm reduction.

The middle section covers the group's programs. The Library Freedom Institute is a cohort-based train-the-trainer course for library workers, backed by a community of practice. Free workshops cover public records, power mapping and open source intelligence, and one-page handouts address law enforcement contact and data brokers. The team also described in-person camps, regional meetings, and consultations on harassment and surveillance self-defense, plus work on vendor contracts with major publishers that now operate as data analytics firms.

The talk closes with a question about right-wing groups seeking seats on library boards and campaigns against Pride displays. The advice was to join boards, attend meetings and speak up, since these efforts are often organized. The speakers also invited technologists to collaborate on usability testing and tools, arguing that libraries are a useful place to reach the public.

talks.title: BADBOX: Behind the Scenes of an Android Supply-Chain Attack
talks.teaser: Traces how malware preinstalled on cheap Android TV boxes grew into a residential proxy botnet sold through major resellers.
talks.summary:
The talk follows BADBOX, a supply-chain operation in which inexpensive, unbranded Android set-top TV boxes reached buyers with malware already installed. The speaker, a technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, explains how a researcher's report led to a purchase and a basic network check that confirmed the box contacted command-and-control servers. Compromised devices could be turned into residential proxies that routed other people's traffic through a buyer's home connection, and the malware could also intercept one-time passwords used to register accounts.

The middle of the talk turns to a wider investigation by a security firm. The malware sat low in the Android runtime, using a Zygote-based design to embed itself in running applications, and it relied on modular components for ad fraud, SMS abuse and silent app installation. A related component called PeachPit affected roughly 121,000 Android and 159,000 iOS devices and generated billions of ad clicks a day. The speaker also walks through detection approaches, including sampling cheap devices, checking known indicators of compromise, inspecting certificates and user agents, and analyzing backbone traffic to estimate scale.

The talk closes with the regulatory response. EFF filed a complaint with the FTC about resellers that kept selling these devices without warning buyers, and it raised questions about accountability and the digital divide, since cheaper devices often lack built-in protections. For practitioners and consumers, the practical lesson is that compromise can happen before a device ever reaches a home, so research into unfamiliar brands and attention from regulators both matter.

talks.title: Telecom in an Exclave
talks.teaser: Explores how a remote U.S. exclave gets its internet and what it would take to upgrade it.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Point Roberts, a small piece of Washington State that sits south of the 49th parallel and can only be reached by water, by air, or by driving through Canada. It begins with the area's telecom history, which was served by Canadian carriers until a U.S. phone company took over in the late 1980s after a regulatory dispute, and then by a cable provider that eventually abandoned its plant.

The middle of the talk covers what residents can actually buy today. Options include DSL topping out around 25 megabits, mobile plans from the two large carriers limited by a single tower and a local height ordinance, and satellite service that struggles with tall trees and low angles to the sky. Two publicly funded fiber projects are described. One stalled when trenching ran into archaeological sites, and the other, an open-access county plan, uses overhead lines on existing poles. A community effort called Point Net proposes lighting up fiber that already lands on the point, paired with Wi-Fi 6 or CBRS wireless.

The talk closes with a call for technical volunteers, since the community project needs people who know wireless and network build-out. The speaker also described the local economy, shrinking population and border dynamics in a bonus section, and then took questions on shipping, banking, housing and local politics. The practical takeaway is that the obstacles on the point are as much about permitting, funding and local coordination as they are about the underlying technology.

talks.title: Less Power to Porn Tech Giants, More Love in the Cyberspace
talks.teaser: Traces a European legal campaign against porn platforms under data and platform rules, alongside research on image-based sexual abuse.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the influence large porn platforms have over how people understand sexuality and their bodies. The speaker, a lawyer and digital rights advocate, presents it as a follow-up to earlier research into biased recommendation systems on one such site, and moves on to a European strategic litigation campaign built on data protection law. The argument is that sexual preference data is sensitive, that viewers were tracked without meaningful consent, and that automated profiling of them is opaque and cannot be challenged.

The campaign reportedly led one major platform to add a consent banner after media attention and regulator statements, and cases have since moved through Italy and Cyprus. Separately, the EU's Digital Services Act led to the designation of very large online platforms, and in late 2023 three porn sites were named, which the companies then challenged in court. A co-presenter shared research on image-based sexual abuse, including non-consensual sharing and deepfakes, the burden victims carry in collecting evidence, and the greater risk to marginalized groups whose digital footprints can be exposed. The Q&A covered how such rules could spread beyond Europe, payment processors as a pressure point, and how slowly platform trust and safety teams respond to reports.

The main takeaway is that lasting change needs regulators, civil society, sex workers, survivors and small ethical builders working together. Practitioners should expect litigation and designation to move slowly, and should treat consent, algorithm transparency and takedown responsiveness as open problems.

talks.title: The Real Danger From AI Is Not the Technology
talks.teaser: Argues that the greatest threat from AI lies in how people and institutions use it, not in the technology itself.

talks.title: Congress's Privacy Wars
talks.teaser: Traces the fight in Congress over warrantless surveillance under Section 702 and the reform efforts that stalled.
talks.summary:
The session, presented by the advocacy group Restore the Fourth, walks through the 2023 and 2024 fight in Congress over the surveillance powers in Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act. It explains the basic structure: the NSA collects communications of foreign targets, which often include Americans, and agencies including the FBI can search that database without a warrant. The speakers cite disclosed court opinions describing improper searches, including queries tied to protest organizers and January 6 events, along with other cases such as searches of dating partners and housing applicants.

The middle of the talk follows the legislative path. A bipartisan reform bill from late 2023 would have required warrants for these searches and addressed the purchase of data, but the House Judiciary version was narrowed and the intelligence committee pushed a weaker proposal of its own. The speakers describe a chaotic rules process, a public claim about Russian nuclear weapons in space that they consider overhyped, and an intense administration lobbying campaign. The warrant amendment failed on a tie broken by the Speaker's vote, and the reauthorization passed with a two-year term.
