The closing takeaway is that the short renewal sets up another round of this fight around the next election, and that the coalition working on the issue will keep pressing offices in both parties. Listeners are encouraged to contact their representatives and watch for the next debate. In the questions, the speakers noted that DHS and border surveillance remain part of the wider picture and that an international cybercrime treaty was a separate matter outside their focus.

talks.title: Hacking at Leaves
talks.teaser: Traces a Colorado hackerspace's COVID relief work against colonial history and Navajo Nation context, followed by a filmmakers' panel.
talks.summary:
This session opens with a screening-linked panel for the documentary Hacking at Leaves, which had its US premiere at the conference. The film follows a small hackerspace in Durango, Colorado, whose members contributed to COVID relief efforts, and places that story within the history of American colonialism and the Navajo Nation. Participants introduced themselves, including filmmaker Johannes Grenzfurthner, producer Jasmin Hagendorfer and Peter Romine, an engineering educator at Navajo Technical University.

Romine described how his program teaches students to build practical projects for their own communities. Examples included a solar-powered medicine cooler designed by a nursing student for a family with no reliable electricity, and an air filter adapted from a box fan to reduce fine dust linked to asthma in Navajo homes. The panel also discussed why the story needed its wider historical context to make sense, and how the team tried to represent Indigenous voices without relying on stereotypes, including the many women involved in hacker circles.

In audience questions, Grenzfurthner addressed why an Austrian filmmaker chose to tell a story about Native American history, arguing that privilege should be used to pass the microphone to others. He also reflected on political labels and framed the film as being about communities, some chosen and some inherited, with solidarity across them as the goal. Attendees also learned where his earlier films could be found.

talks.title: What Wi-Fi Devices Are Nearby? Any Cameras Watching Me?
talks.teaser: Shows how a monitor-mode Wi-Fi tool maps nearby devices and reveals cameras uploading video without joining their networks.
talks.summary:
Caleb Madrigal opens with a refresher on Wi-Fi as a radio technology. Networks sit on channels in the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands, and the talk focuses on the data link layer, where MAC addresses identify network interfaces. He explains monitor mode, which receives frames without joining a network. Traffic captured this way stays encrypted, but frame headers still expose addresses, frame types, network names and received signal strength.

The motivation was a home camera that kept uploading video while it was disarmed, which led him to build trackerjacker, an open-source Python tool. The demo covers a mapping mode that hops across channels and records networks, connected devices, power levels and vendor prefixes into a YAML file. He also shows the plugin interface, including a fox-hunting plugin that follows the strongest signal and a plugin that counts device manufacturers.

He closes with practical takeaways. Vendor information makes it possible to spot particular cameras and other devices without connecting to their networks, and bursts of upload traffic can reveal activity. Phones leak identifiers through probe requests. Randomized addresses help until a device connects, so turning Wi-Fi off while travelling reduces exposure. The tool currently runs only on Linux, and he recommends external adapters for monitor mode.

talks.title: Psychoactive Drugs: How They Hack the Brain and What It Means for Our Minds
talks.teaser: Explains how psychoactive drugs act on brain receptors and critically reviews the MDMA-for-PTSD trial controversy.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a pharmacist's walkthrough of how neurons pass signals across synapses using neurotransmitters, receptors and reuptake pumps, and how drugs can interfere at each step. Opioids serve as the first example, covering pain relief, respiratory depression and how naloxone displaces them at the receptor. The speaker then addresses fentanyl's potency, arguing that dosing errors in illicit supply drive overdoses more than any airborne danger, and that fears spread through police training and media were not supported by how the drug behaves.

The middle section covers cannabis, which remains federally scheduled despite state-level changes, with thin evidence for many claimed uses and little product verification. Serotonergic psychedelics and ecstasy are explained next, along with ketamine's rapid antidepressant effect. The central case study is MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD. Despite a large reported effect in phase three trials, an FDA advisory panel voted against approval. The speaker walks through the problems: functional unblinding, a participant pool with prior drug use, dropouts in follow-up, concerns about therapist conduct and touch, and a reported sexual assault in an earlier trial.

The closing message is that a strong effect does not prove a drug safe or effective, and that medical use needs consistent risk and benefit evidence. Listeners are encouraged to test claims about drugs critically. Questions afterward covered trial dosing, comparisons with stimulants, and finding reliable harm reduction information.

talks.title: Working Towards a Sneakernet for Libre Biotech Wetware
talks.teaser: Covers efforts toward offline, physical sharing of libre biotech wetware designs.

talks.title: Hack the Violin: A Hacker's Approach to Learning, Playing, and Teaching the Violin
talks.teaser: Applies a hacker's step-by-step thinking to the violin, covering bowing, left-hand setup, listening and practice habits.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that poor beginner violin sound is not inevitable and that traditional rote-learning methods often cause it. The speaker presents a set of ordered "hacks," small procedures that run in a fixed sequence, much like code that must be in place before a program can run. Each hack targets a step that students commonly miss or underemphasize.

The hacks follow the order in which a player needs them. Singing the musical idea before playing brings the sound into the body, and using the ears to guide the hands keeps the player listening. For the left hand, the fingers set on the string before the bow moves, with grip kept to weight rather than pressure. For the right hand, the bow is balanced on the string, started from a still position, and pulled in one smooth, progressive stroke, with a pivot used for string crossings. Practice advice covers checking the left hand when trouble appears, using simple physical changes such as walking or standing on one leg to break tension, linking notes together, and practicing specifically while performing generally. Equipment advice stresses good strings and fresh bow hair.

The session ends with a sequence for producing a sweeter tone: hold an intention for the sound, transfer it through touch at the points of contact, and sing the idea first. The speaker stresses that focused practice matters more than long, unfocused sessions and that the hacks supplement rather than replace practice.

talks.title: A Revolution in Representation: Computation Comes to Democracy's Aid
talks.teaser: Shows how the open-source Polis deliberation system helps groups find shared ground and how governments and movements use it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a recap of a workshop on group decision-making and governance held the night before, then traces the speaker's background in participatory projects. These ranged from street-level listening experiments and open-science work to the 2014 protests in Taiwan and the civic technologists who followed. It introduces Polis, an AGPL-licensed deliberation system created in 2012, which presents participants with short statements they can agree with, disagree with or pass on, and then maps the resulting opinion groups.

The middle of the talk covers case studies at national and local scale. These include Taiwan's V Taiwan process, a climate assembly in Austria, a ballot-related deliberation in Uruguay, a Slovak civil society effort to counter misinformation, a UK government policy lab, and a multinational youth consultation tied to a UN climate summit. The speaker explains the comment routing that decides which statements each person sees, how consensus statements and bridging across clusters are read, and why outreach, framing and moderation matter as much as the software itself.

The closing section takes audience questions on censorship, identity checks, reaching rural and marginalised communities, and whether results can carry binding power. The speaker argues that tools placed between citizens and their governments should be open source so that independent oversight remains possible. Practitioners are encouraged to consider how the tools they already build could support collective decisions.

talks.title: Innovating for Impact: Building Technology in Resource-Constrained Environments
talks.teaser: Explains how a nonprofit tech lab builds software on tight budgets through partnerships and resourcefulness.
talks.summary:
Jason A. Long, who heads the tech group known as the Innovation Lab at the human rights organization Human Rights First, speaks with interviewer Alexander Urbelis about building software for a nonprofit with little money. He recounts moving from a coding bootcamp into a fellowship after realizing technologists can work in impact-focused roles. He describes the lab as an enabling partner that embeds with internal and outside teams to find where technology can expand their reach.

Project examples include Glimpse, a computer vision platform that flags violent actions and objects in large video archives so investigators can avoid reviewing footage by hand. An asylum intake assistant keeps a human in the loop, and a legislation tracker summarizes bills and votes across government levels. A university hackathon produced a debate tool that generates likely candidate answers from public records.

For constrained teams, his advice centers on coalitions, creativity and relationships: partner with better-resourced groups that share a mission, get to know cloud account managers, and look for donated compute. He also said the lab avoids shipping tools with known dangers to at-risk users, is working toward open-sourcing projects, and welcomes security feedback, since nonprofits are frequent attack targets. Students and volunteers were invited to contribute.

talks.title: Robot Invasion! The Rise of Educational Robotics
talks.teaser: Surveys educational robots for kids, from screen-free codable models to block-based and Python-based options.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys the growing range of educational robots available to teachers and parents, from kindergarten through college. The speaker organizes the options by coding approach, starting with self-contained robots that need no device at all, then moving to block-based coding and finally to robots that teach script code such as Python.

Live demonstrations covered screen-free models that read snap-on or colour-coded tiles, including a robot aimed at early elementary grades that can dance and turn in 45-degree steps, and a track-based system that can be extended toward Python. Block-based options such as Dash, which accepts Lego attachments and offers flowchart and block apps, were shown alongside Python-oriented robots like Edison, a low-cost option that scans barcodes and has its own Python-like environment, and Pixel, which walks beginners through step-by-step Python lessons in an app.

The speaker closed with buying guidance: tactile screen-free robots suit the youngest learners, Dash was named the most versatile for grades three to five, and Edison offered the best value, though it needs AAA batteries. For learners new to hardware, the speaker suggested snap-circuit kits as a gentler step before Arduino. The main takeaway is to choose a robot based on the child's age, prior coding experience and budget.

talks.title: Pwn Chromebook With Linux
talks.teaser: Shows how to replace Chrome OS on old Chromebooks with Linux by removing firmware write protection and flashing boot firmware.
talks.summary:
A father and security analyst describes why he began repurposing used Chromebooks bought for his children. Their installed Chrome OS versions had reached end of support, and the small soldered storage made the machines feel disposable. He frames the project around update policies, data tracking concerns, and the e-waste that school Chromebooks generate, and gives a brief history of the platform from its 2011 debut to its rise in classrooms.

The main section walks through the workflow: checking hardware specifications, removing firmware write protection (a screw on older models, the battery on a newer one, with the Suzy-Q cable method noted as an alternative), enabling developer mode, flashing a full ROM firmware, and booting Linux from USB. Ubuntu struggled on the limited hardware, while Gallium OS and Linux Lite installed more reliably on the older units. Audio problems recurred, and one model lost sound after a firmware change. He also shares another user's boot loop story and demonstrates Doom running on one machine.

He closes with practical lessons: confirm hardware compatibility before buying, document each step, and back up stock firmware before flashing. Involving his children in removing screws gave them hands-on exposure to hardware work. Attendees were reminded that these steps can void warranties and should only be applied to devices they own.

talks.title: Ham Radio for Hackers
talks.teaser: Surveys hobbyist radio projects, from low-cost SDR and Pico-based gear to balloons and satellites, plus the steps to get licensed.
talks.summary:
Dan Romanchik opens by framing amateur radio under the US rules in Part 97, whose stated purposes include experimentation and advancing the radio art. He argues that licensed operators get more power, more modes and more room to experiment than users of GMRS or Citizens Band. Low-cost software-defined radios built around a Raspberry Pi show how the hobby is moving toward hardware and software tinkering.

The middle section surveys projects. Building antennas is cheap, and homebrew copies of commercial designs can cost a fraction of the store-bought price because antenna physics has not changed. Arduino and Raspberry Pi Pico projects, such as a Morse keyer, show a shift toward microcontrollers. Amateur satellites date back to 1961, and some hobbyists track cheap helium balloons carrying radio trackers around the world. Digital voice efforts such as M17 and FreeDV aim for fully open designs, funded by the ARDC, which was created from a sold-off block of IP addresses. GNU Radio provides a signal-processing toolkit, and speculative AI uses, such as a voice assistant for band conditions, close the list.

The talk ends with licensing. There are three US classes, each requiring an exam that can be taken for free, with a study guide available online and a fee for a ten-year license. The Q&A covered limits such as the ban on encrypted transmissions, with satellite command as an exception, and whether to publish hotspot locations. The takeaway is that experimenting within the rules is the point, and local clubs and the ham radio village offer a way in.

talks.title: Flights of Fancy: Celebrating the Dead Ends of the Jet Engine Revolution
talks.teaser: Traces the failed engine designs and overlooked ideas that eventually produced the modern jet engine.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with how ordinary jet airliners have become, then asks the audience to imagine inventing a jet engine in the early 1900s. It separates true reaction engines from propellers and lays out the core problems of early aviation: piston engines were heavy for the power they produced, lost output at altitude, and could not simply gain power by adding cylinders.

The middle traces a sequence of attempts that stalled. Turbochargers and turbo-compounding helped at altitude, while ramjets, pulse jets and motor-jet hybrids proved inefficient. A 1928 government report judged simple jet propulsion uncompetitive, which the speaker presents as a lesson in how confident verdicts can be wrong. Progress came once aerodynamic turbine theory and metallurgy caught up, enabling the designs of Whittle and von Ohain and German wartime engines that were limited by high-temperature materials. A hydrogen-fueled high-altitude engine was never flown, yet its fuel pump later informed a rocket engine.

The closing argument is that the jet engine emerged from many partial ideas, materials and wartime economics converging at the right moment, and that ideas alone were not enough. The speaker encourages builders to keep experimenting, since some outcomes can only be learned by doing the work. Audience questions covered how to allocate development resources and the prop fan.

talks.title: Explosive Overflow: Lessons From Rocket Science
talks.teaser: Traces the Ariane 5 failure to reused code and design assumptions, then draws product security lessons on static analysis and memory safety.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits the 1996 maiden flight of the Ariane 5 rocket, which self-destructed about 39 seconds after liftoff. The speaker traces the failure to an inertial reference module carried over unchanged from the earlier Ariane 4. A velocity value that the faster new rocket produced overflowed a narrower integer type. The error handler shut the unit down, the identical backup failed the same way, and the flight computer read the diagnostic data as real velocity, forcing the vehicle off course.

The speaker lists the contributing causes: reused legacy code, untested design assumptions, an alignment routine that kept running after liftoff although it was no longer needed, and exception handling that treated software errors as random hardware faults. The talk then turns to what it means to prove software correct. It covers formal verification, including its cost and limits, the halting problem, and Gödel's incompleteness results. It also compares memory-safe languages, noting Ada's earlier mandate for critical weapons systems and the practical difficulty of rewriting large C and C++ codebases.

For practitioners, the main takeaways are to triage static analysis output instead of handing developers thousands of raw findings, to enable compiler sanitizers even in legacy projects, and to make secure defaults and vetted libraries the easy path. The Q&A also touched on seL4 and fuzzing tools. The overall message is to treat reused code and undocumented assumptions as risks that need testing against realistic inputs.

talks.title: Incubated Machine Learning Exploits: Backdooring ML Pipelines w/Input-Handling Bugs
talks.teaser: Shows how input-handling bugs can be used to backdoor machine learning pipelines.

talks.title: Our Defensive Security Blind Spot
talks.teaser: Shows how inline classification of sensitive data in service proxies can flag data leaving a system in real time.
talks.summary:
Wesley Hales starts from the gap in current defenses. Perimeter tools such as WAFs and API security products rely heavily on signatures and mostly inspect request headers and a small slice of the body, so they miss much of the sensitive data that leaves an environment in responses and outbound calls. He points to recent edge-device exploits and large data leaks as evidence, and describes the data flows in production that go unmonitored, including web submissions, third-party egress and logging.

The core of the talk is an approach that runs inline inside the service proxy, Envoy in his examples, using small WebAssembly modules written in Rust. These modules classify fields such as card numbers, Social Security numbers and bank routing numbers in both requests and responses. Checks include pattern rejects, checksum validation such as Luhn for card numbers, and recognition of structured JSON keys, with asynchronous reconciliation against an existing DLP tool where more certainty is needed. Results are exported to Prometheus and Grafana. A live demo showed spikes in the dashboard when a page containing fake identifiers was loaded. He also covered detecting exploit output, such as command results appearing in responses, and a case study of an airline scraper, where response-based signals enabled rate limiting and the scraper was eventually blocked.

The takeaway is that watching what data services emit, how much, and in what pattern can reveal exfiltration, lateral movement and exploitation that IP reputation and signatures miss. He noted that the components are open source, including a proxy SDK for writing custom classification modules, and asked for feedback on a talk he was giving for the first time.

talks.title: Strength in Unity: Sharing Is Caring
talks.teaser: Makes the case for open-source threat intelligence sharing between public and private sectors, using MISP and OpenCTI as examples.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that government agencies, companies and individuals face the same cyber threats and should pool what they know instead of working in isolation. The speaker points to large past incidents such as SolarWinds and WannaCry, saying responders who compared notes could connect the campaigns and act faster. Information sharing between government and industry is described as slow and cautious, with sensitive material often passed along by email.

To address the cost barrier, the speaker walks through a fully open-source pipeline, explained through a garden metaphor. Raw logs from sources such as firewalls and intrusion detection systems feed into the Elastic stack, which handles storage, search and dashboards. OpenCTI then organizes the data and supports attribution of threat actors, and MISP serves as the exchange where indicators such as IP addresses, domains and file hashes are shared with other organizations.

In the question period, the speaker explained that MISP and OpenCTI let organizations control who can see their intelligence, so they can keep it private or publish it. The tools are free and available on GitHub. The closing message is that shared intelligence, pooled expertise and low-cost tooling help organizations detect and respond to threats more quickly, and that teams without a dedicated SOC can benefit as well.

talks.title: Right to Repair in California - Using New Legislation for DIY Wheelchair Repair
talks.teaser: Explains how California's SB 244 right to repair law can help disabled users obtain wheelchair parts and service documentation.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a power wheelchair user who has repaired his own chairs since 2012, opens by arguing that durable medical equipment is built around insurance billing rather than repair. He describes high parts prices, missing error codes, closed documentation, and repair shops that would rather bill for a replacement device. He places this alongside wider right to repair disputes, including a farm equipment case, to show the movement's reach.

The middle of the talk walks through California's SB 244, which took effect in July 2024. He explains the parts availability windows tied to product price, the duty to provide service manuals, diagrams and error codes on fair terms, and the carve-outs for farm equipment, video game devices, alarm systems and products sold before mid-2021. He flags a loophole for manufacturers that repair their own products and criticizes a separate bill that would exclude wheelchair batteries, joysticks and other components. He then recounts his own dealings with a manufacturer: after a polite email requesting error codes and a maintenance manual, he received documents and a parts shipment, but firmware, battery communication details and mechanical drawings were refused.

He closes with practical advice. Check whether a product falls within the law's date range, use precise terms such as service manual and error code, and keep a written paper trail by email rather than public posts. Because private lawsuits are not allowed under the law, complaints go to a district attorney's office. He points listeners to iFixit and EFF resources and a state-by-state tracker for pending legislation.

talks.title: Get High Like Planes: Combining Psychology, Social Engineering, and AI
talks.teaser: Shows how red teams combine psychological pretexting with voice cloning and generative AI lures in a social engineering engagement.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with classic social engineering principles, such as pretexting, social proof, authority, reciprocity, urgency, liking and baiting, and how they played out in physical intrusions at banks and credit unions. The speakers also outline how people lean on hearing, seeing or doing when they process information, and how a pretext can be worded to match that preference.

Next, the speakers review how voice cloning has developed and compare open-source tools with commercial services. They report that the open-source options they tried needed heavy GPU hardware and sounded robotic, so they used a commercial service for a remote red team engagement. The case study covered an insurance-sector client, where a spoofed CEO email with a video lure and a cloned voice asked staff to make paper airplanes. Around 11 percent of the targeted staff completed the full chain, and the speakers extrapolated the potential financial impact.

For defense, they discussed cryptographic signing of media, rotating keyword verification, AI-based detection, secret sharing, and positive training incentives, and noted that each has limits in an ongoing arms race. Practitioners should take away that obvious red flags, such as an external-sender banner, are often ignored when a message seems to come from a trusted executive, and that voice samples for cloning can be pulled from public earnings call audio.

talks.title: Social Justice and Prompt Engineering: What We Know So Far
talks.teaser: Surveys research on how prompt wording shapes bias in LLM outputs and text-to-image models, with practical mitigation ideas.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short primer on prompt engineering, covering few-shot examples and chain-of-thought prompting. It then argues that large language models absorb the prejudices in their training data, so the way a request is worded can reduce harm for both users and builders.

Several recent studies are reviewed. One audit of a commercial model posed yes-or-no decisions about hypothetical applicants and found demographic skews; telling the model that discrimination is illegal and to ignore protected traits worked best. Another study found far less bias when models judged one candidate in isolation than when they compared two, and that instructions to treat groups equally cut bias. Supplying outside data, such as a market price, reduced lowball offers tied to a seller's name. Text-to-image studies showed skewed portraits, uneven quality and refusals on sensitive prompts, and multilingual prompts shifted results depending on grammatical gender.

The speaker also replicated a reference-letter study, where men were described by achievements and women by personality, and found that added context and fairness instructions moved the output toward parity. The takeaways: keep high-stakes decisions away from models without human review, ask for absolute rather than relative judgments, anchor prompts with external data, and remember that removing names is not enough because models infer identity from other cues. Expect outputs to shift with small wording changes, and avoid lock-in to a single vendor.

talks.title: Net Who-trality: Revisiting the FCC Fake Comment Scandal
talks.teaser: Traces how public records requests and server logs were used to identify who submitted millions of fake net neutrality comments.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits the flood of comments sent to the FCC in 2017 while the agency weighed rolling back net neutrality rules. The speaker says roughly 18 million of the roughly 22 million comments were later confirmed fake, and that millions carried real people's names without their consent. Before getting to the investigation, the talk gives a short history of net neutrality, covering the 1934 Communications Act, the Title I and Title II split, and the 2015 Open Internet Order, and explains why the current legal fight is still unsettled.

The core of the talk is how the speaker tried to trace the comments to their sources. Freedom of Information Act requests to the FCC and the General Services Administration for API keys, submission logs and bulk CSV uploads were refused at first, which led to a lawsuit, partial court rulings and a settlement. The speaker walks through the data formats, the gap between timestamps in the API system and the comment system, and the fuzzy matching used to link submissions to the people and organizations behind them. Attribution relied on shared IP addresses, email domains, API key registration details and open-source lookups.

The talk closes with a search site built on the released data. It links to each comment on the FCC's own website instead of republishing personal details. The speaker notes that the fake submissions were easy to spot because they were sloppy, that more careful campaigns would be harder to trace, and that people should not trust comments they cannot verify.

talks.title: From Hackerspace to Hackerhome
talks.teaser: Chronicles how a Madison, Wisconsin hackerspace grew from a shoestring startup into a volunteer-run, self-owned workshop.
talks.summary:
Chris Meyer, founder of the Sector67 hackerspace in Madison, Wisconsin, traces the group's path from a 2010 business plan contest entry to a self-owned building. Early on, the group ran small community events such as soldering workshops held at a university, then rented a former lawnmower repair shop with a personal guarantee on the lease. A landlord's redevelopment plan forced a move, and a three-year effort to partner with an insurance company ended when its goals did not line up with the space's.

The group then decided it had to own its home. Savings from years of unpaid founder salary, plus a crowdfunding campaign that drew around 118 donors, covered the purchase of a 1949 warehouse and the cost of lifting its roof. The talk covers the harder parts of the build: a late-night propane tank accident that sent the founder to hospital, while volunteers kept the project moving; occupancy and fire-rating rules; concrete work in freezing weather; and salvaging building materials to cut costs.

The finances stayed free of loans, with memberships as the main income and eBay resale of surplus stock adding more. Meyer closes with practical advice: tie training to specific tasks, expect entrepreneurship to be hard, and look at community "third place" writing when planning a shared space.

talks.title: Popping S(h)ells - Hunting for Vulns in the Stock Market
talks.teaser: Explains how stock exchange design assumptions create exploitable gaps, and walks through SEC-prosecuted market manipulation cases.
talks.summary:
Eric Bryce, who works in algorithmic trading, opens by framing the talk as an introduction to how market manipulation works and why it tends to get caught. He notes that enforcement records are unusually rich, and that many cases surface years after the conduct, once regulators have the full trade data.

The middle of the talk covers mechanics. He walks through limit order books, the FIX messaging format used to send orders, and why latency between the New Jersey data centers matters, including why microwave links can beat fiber. He then explains adverse selection and how a large resting bid or offer can signal false intent. Spoofing and layering are the main examples, including a metals trading desk case prosecuted years after the conduct. He also covers dark pool midpoint pricing abused with fake quotes, rigging of the LIBOR benchmark through coordinated submissions, and cornering futures markets such as silver and orange juice.

He closes by stressing that the data retained by exchanges makes detection likely, since a losing counterparty often reviews the tape and reports suspicious orders. Questions covered whistleblower incentives, leveraged options in insider cases, and cross-asset manipulation. The practical takeaway is that understanding how exchanges are built helps explain both how schemes work and how they are found.

talks.title: AI Made a 0-Day: Noah Get the Boat
talks.teaser: Shows how generative AI helped produce a working RCE payload, a captcha bypass and other attack chains against web apps.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the view that generative AI should augment hacking rather than replace the human. The speaker frames the discussion around context, explaining how transformer models apply layered knowledge, and argues that a beginner's mind matters when prompting these tools. It separates predictable tool orchestration, where a model chooses the next scanner to run, from more open-ended generative work.

The middle of the talk walks through redacted case studies. An error in a report-generating web app became a remote code execution payload, and a model produced a working one-line version in a single attempt after days of manual research. Other cases covered a browser automation script that located form fields with validation gaps to build cross-site scripting payloads, a model suggesting an uncommon SQL technique to pull records past a web application firewall, and OCR of a captcha chained with an anti-CSRF token request to automate logins. The speaker also described gaming a search ranking system to surface weaker sites, and prompt injection used to coax a model into returning a protected file.

The closing takeaways stress that the human remains central, since the model's output is non-deterministic and results need checking. The speaker recommends keeping attack chaining creative, reserving AI for tasks that truly need it, and using private or local models to avoid content filter problems. The talk ends with a call to protect diversity of thought in how people use these tools.

talks.title: Using the J Language to Streamline Hacking
talks.teaser: Presents the J programming language as a way to streamline hacking tasks.

talks.title: Hacking Your Health: Adventures in Building a Glucose Monitor
talks.teaser: Walks through how a continuous glucose monitor senses blood sugar, from enzyme chemistry to circuit boards and wireless links.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a high school student on a skills competition team, opens with why glucose monitoring matters. He points to the millions of people with diabetes, the high cost of continuous monitors for people without coverage, and the appeal of cheaper alternatives. He then explains the core chemistry: an enzyme taken from a common mold reacts with glucose and oxygen to produce hydrogen peroxide, and the peroxide's conductivity can be measured and mapped to a glucose level through calibration.

The middle of the talk covers the team's homemade prototype. They built a large, crude sensor from two copper electrodes with a foam membrane soaked in the enzyme, then tested it in sugar water and reported a strong correlation across only a few measurements. Design goals followed: low power draw, measurement frequency balanced against battery life, a wireless link in the ISM band with strong encryption, and a protocol such as Bluetooth Low Energy or LoRa. Energy harvesting was explored as a battery alternative. He also described laying out a circuit board in open-source KiCad, ordering boards from a low-cost manufacturer, and the soldering problems that followed.

He closes by stating the prototypes were non-functional and that the enzyme is consumed, which would require periodic replacement. The total budget was about 300 dollars. The main takeaway is how much chemistry, electronics and wireless engineering sits inside these devices. The question period touched on regulatory approval, NFC power, and non-invasive sensing.

talks.title: Modern Day Automobile Safety: Rescue Ops Using CanBus
talks.teaser: Shows how standardized commands on a vehicle's CAN bus could help firefighters stabilize, access and extricate crash victims.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with vehicle extrication, the work of freeing people from crashed cars. The presenter, a long-serving firefighter and fire instructor, explains how modern design slows rescuers: crumple zones that can reach fuel tanks, boron steel pillars, electronic doors, and manual releases drivers rarely know. Crash fires and airbags or fobs that keep a car active add risk.

Next he covers drive-by-wire controls and the CAN bus that relays commands between sensors and actuators. The protocol is standard, but each maker defines its own commands. He proposes three standard modes built from existing commands: stabilization, which sets the parking brake and cuts power or fuel; access, which disables airbags, unlocks doors and lowers windows; and egress, which adjusts seats and the steering column. Safeguards would include a crash-sensor gate, one-way state changes and fob control through a dispatch-held lockbox.

He acknowledges obstacles. Regulators may treat new triggers as new features needing long road testing, and manufacturers see little commercial reason to act. Context matters, since automatic seat movement would be unsafe with a passenger trapped nearby. He suggests firmware updates could deliver the batched commands without new parts, and mentions a provisional patent to keep the approach open. The takeaway is that the capability largely exists; the hard parts are standards, testing and manufacturer buy-in.

talks.title: PortableSecret - Carry and Share Your Most Critical Secrets Without Special Software
talks.teaser: Shows how to wrap secrets in a self-contained HTML file that opens in any browser without special software.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a gap: people who are not comfortable with GPG or private keys still need to exchange sensitive items such as a door code or a scanned passport. Common messengers and email expose that content to platform operators, and anyone with brief access to a phone can read it. The proposed fix is PortableSecret, a single HTML file holding an encrypted payload and a small amount of script. The recipient opens it in any modern browser, online or offline, and enters a password to view the content.

The cryptography relies on standard primitives exposed through the browser's Web Crypto interface: AES in GCM mode for confidentiality and integrity, and a password-based key derivation function run for many iterations to slow guessing attacks. The talk walks through the file layout, a live decryption, and a creator tool. It also covers the design's assumptions and weak points, including poor passwords, guessable password hints, and tampered copies, and notes that keyloggers and compromised systems are outside what any file can protect against.

Practical use cases include keeping a backup decryption key on several USB drives, publishing an encrypted passport copy as a retrievable page, and leaving family instructions for worst-case scenarios. Other examples include sharing temporary SSH keys and sending messages from a borrowed phone. The Q&A covered iOS handling, file size limits caused by URL encoding, and USB drive longevity. The takeaway is that a simple, open design can give non-technical people a practical privacy layer.

talks.title: Strengthening Security Culture Through Compassion and Understanding
talks.teaser: Explains how compassion and non-punitive responses can build a security culture where employees report mistakes early.
talks.summary:
Davis, a security compliance engineer at amazee.io, argues that people are often the weakest link in a security program and that annual awareness training alone does not change behavior. He explains how a punitive environment leads staff to hide mistakes, skip incident reports, and see security as an opponent. He breaks fear into several forms, such as fear of punishment, blame, judgment, and uncertainty, and ties each one to costs like delayed reporting and lost trust.

The core of the talk is compassion as a practical approach: empathy, patience, a non-judgmental stance, and encouragement for people who report problems. Examples include treating a first error as an honest accident, thanking staff who flag phishing emails, sending short monthly security briefings, and having leaders follow the same rules. He points to Google's move to hardware security keys, Netscape's early bug bounty, and Microsoft's secure development lifecycle as cases where fixing root causes worked better than blaming people.

He closes by arguing that rewarding early reporting and treating mistakes as lessons leads to earlier detection and fewer successful attacks. Audience questions covered motivational coaching, linking work security habits to personal life, and using gamification to engage staff.

talks.title: Making Surveillance Policy Change in Canada: Slow Burns and Sudden Actions
talks.teaser: Traces how access-to-information requests exposed Canadian federal use of mobile phone forensic tools and led to policy action.
talks.summary:
Evan Light, a communication researcher at York University, describes a multi-year project to map state surveillance capabilities in Canada and the laws that govern them. Inspired by the EFF's Atlas of Surveillance, the team files access-to-information requests for federal procurement records. Federal requests proved cheap and fast compared with provincial and municipal ones, and many came back with few redactions. The talk also touches on exemptions in the radio communications act that let the RCMP operate outside interference rules during major events.

The central case study concerns mobile forensic devices sold by vendors such as Cellebrite, Magnet Forensics and Grayshift. Contract records showed more than a dozen federal agencies buying these tools, and in many cases the government had skipped the privacy impact assessments its own directives required. A journalist at Radio-Canada reported the findings, and a parliamentary committee quickly held hearings. Agency witnesses described their use, consent and warrant practices, and the committee heard that few agencies had meaningful transparency or reporting mechanisms.

In the closing section, Light outlines recommendations: give federal privacy regulators stronger enforcement powers and a role in procurement, retroactively inventory invasive tools, close the disclosure gap for product demos, and speed up information requests. He ends with practical advice for activists and researchers, including working with journalists and unions, and treating legislators as people who need expert evidence to govern well.

talks.title: There's Always HOPE for Privacy: Policy Wins and Needs
talks.teaser: Reviews FTC privacy enforcement cases and explains how the public can help push for stronger privacy rules.
talks.summary:
Mean Gene opens by framing privacy as ongoing work that anyone can contribute to, from personal habits and helping others to advocacy, art, and local policy groups. The discussion then turns to Ben Weisman, a lawyer in the Federal Trade Commission's privacy division, who explains that the agency enforces consumer protection law against deceptive and unfair data practices, using both case enforcement and industry-wide rulemaking.

The middle of the discussion covers why notice-and-consent policies have fallen short and what enforcement responses the agency has pursued. Examples include health apps and tracking pixels that sent medical information to advertisers, a browsing-data case that required deletion of derived models, bans on selling precise location data tied to sensitive places, and a facial recognition case against a pharmacy chain that brought a five-year ban and stricter testing requirements. Data minimization obligations and ongoing compliance reporting are described as ways to hold companies accountable.

The closing segment gives practical steps: submit complaints through the agency's reporting site, comment on proposed rules and requests for information, and press Congress for comprehensive federal privacy legislation. For practitioners, the takeaway is to use internal product and compliance channels, learn the relevant regulations, and bring those arguments to company leadership.

talks.title: Animism and Artificial Intelligence: A Practical Guide
talks.teaser: Explores how animist beliefs about souls in objects can inform ethical thinking about computers and AI systems.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining animism as a set of beliefs found across many cultures, in which people, places, objects and creatures are regarded as having a life essence. The speaker notes that the term began as an anthropological label, describes its relational side around stewardship, ancestry and mutual obligation, and argues that the outlook can be applied to computing as well.

The middle section traces computer history, from room-sized mainframes and lab machines to personal computers, networked servers and cloud data centres, where hardware becomes interchangeable and people relate to it less personally. It then follows the lineage of AI from rule-based systems and the 1960s chatbot ELIZA through statistical machine learning to large language models, explaining how pretraining, fine-tuning and human feedback shape the assistants people use today. Examples include a stuck container ship, treated as a whole-system problem involving software, weather, workers and cargo, and legal cases that gave rivers and wild rice rights-holding standing.

The closing part offers practical takeaways: evaluate AI as a complete system that includes humans rather than only the model, let ethics guidelines account for relationships and stewardship, experiment with open-source models, and explore collaborative storytelling and creative uses. The speaker argues that sentience does not need to be settled before acting responsibly, and closes by urging people to shape the technology together.

talks.title: Navigating Geopolitical Nuances in Cyberattacks With Advanced IP Address Analysis
talks.teaser: Analyzes RDP honeynet login attempts to test how well proxy-detection services reveal the true origin of attackers.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how attackers reach exposed Windows Remote Desktop servers and whether their real origin can be inferred from IP addresses alone. The researchers ran a cloud-hosted honeynet of RDP servers for several years, capturing brute-force login attempts before compromise and recording attacker sessions afterward. Their starting point is that offender behavior is linked to where offenders operate, but proxies, VPNs and compromised machines blur that link.

To judge proxy use, the team queried several IP reputation services and compared their flags against a ground-truth set. That set was built from mismatches between external and internal addresses and time zones seen in successful intrusions. On a three-month subset, the results showed that the services disagreed widely: one was highly precise but flagged few addresses, while another flagged many and was often wrong. Proxy users tended to route through infrastructure close to themselves, some password habits clustered by country, and attack intensity varied widely even within a single country.

The speakers stressed limits. Compromised intermediate machines can hide the true source, and some services appeared to hold stale or polluted data. Their practical takeaway is that reputation feeds should be treated with caution, especially when attributing activity to a country. Similar tooling and strategies appearing across countries may hint at shared infrastructure, though the evidence they presented is limited. Their next step is to study the kinds of crime carried out inside compromised sessions.

talks.title: Harvest: The Most Interesting Computer You Never Heard Of
talks.teaser: Traces the history and unusual design of Harvest, a one-off IBM machine built for NSA codebreaking in the early 1960s.
talks.summary:
Peter Capek covers Harvest, a unique IBM 7950 developed for the NSA to handle codebreaking and text work. Harvest was an add-on to IBM's Stretch (7030) and operated on the same memory. The talk places it in the context of early transistorized machines, when computing was batch-oriented and data storage relied mostly on tape.

The middle of the talk covers the design. Harvest treated memory as one long string of bits and used two streaming units to pull variable-width bytes from memory, pass them to table lookup and logic units, and write results back. Match units could trigger actions at roughly thirty points in the machine. The tape subsystem, called Tractor, was an unusually fast cassette library, and the talk describes Alpha, the specialized programming notation used to drive the hardware.

The closing section covers the machine's history. It ran from 1962 to 1976, when mechanical wear on the tape system ended its service, and IBM later bought it back after a congressional push for public bids. The takeaway is how much engineering and funding went into custom cryptanalytic hardware, and how many of its ideas, such as standardized I/O and byte-oriented addressing, shaped later IBM designs.

talks.title: Safeguarding Secrets: Homomorphic Encryption for the Curious Mind
talks.teaser: Explains how fully homomorphic encryption lets third parties compute on encrypted data, with a medical imaging case study.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the core idea of homomorphic encryption: a data owner encrypts a value, a service provider performs arithmetic on the ciphertext, and only the owner can decrypt the result. A simple addition example makes this concrete before the speaker traces the field's history. The walk-through moves from early partially homomorphic schemes, which support only one operation, to somewhat homomorphic schemes that accumulate noise with each multiplication, and then to the 2009 bootstrapping technique that showed fully homomorphic encryption was achievable.

The middle of the talk covers arithmetic circuits as the building blocks for complex computation, and how vector-based libraries use SIMD operations and rotations to speed things up. The main case study adapts ResNet-50, a convolutional neural network, so it can run on encrypted CT images to flag a large vessel occlusion stroke. The speaker explained how image data is packed into ciphertext vectors to make convolutions workable. The reported encrypted version ran around 50,000 times slower and needed roughly 16,000 times more memory than the plaintext model, requiring a large cluster.

The closing section lists open problems: usability of existing libraries, hardware and GPU acceleration, and compilers that could automatically convert plaintext algorithms into encrypted equivalents. The takeaway for practitioners is that the technique is becoming viable for narrow workloads where its overhead is acceptable, and that continued fundamental research is needed before it is practical at broader scale.

talks.title: Cap2r: Rescuing the Forgotten Texts Hidden in Analog Video
talks.teaser: Shows how forgotten texts hidden in analog video signals can be recovered and preserved.

talks.title: The Arduboy Story
talks.teaser: Traces how a business-card project grew into the Arduboy open-source handheld and the community of game developers around it.
talks.summary:
Kevin Bates introduces the Arduboy, a credit-card-sized open-source game system built on an Arduino-compatible microcontroller with a small monochrome OLED screen. He explains that it started as a hobbyist's business card that played Tetris, which drew wide online attention and pushed him to turn it into a product. He walks through the early path: prototyping, showing units at a maker fair, joining a hardware accelerator based in Shenzhen, and working with factories on molds, buttons and hand assembly.

The middle of the talk covers the difficult steps of production. A first Kickstarter funded the initial run, while retail talks with a large chain showed how return and buy-back terms make wholesale risky for a small maker. After production stalled during a chip shortage, a community member added external memory to the device, and the company then released an expanded version. Community work is central to the project: hundreds of free games, tools for simulation and debugging, a moderated forum that answers questions quickly, and a special edition whose profits were shared with the developers who made the artwork.

He closes by arguing that the project's success rests on a design that invites tinkering, on openness to outside contributions, and on a forum where people help each other. He notes that the company has never been profitable and is considering selling or taking outside investment. He frames the work as a way to teach programming, critical thinking and problem solving through play.

talks.title: Privacy-Focused Computing Curriculum for Teens
talks.teaser: Presents a middle school curriculum on privacy, internet infrastructure, and how governments and companies control digital systems.
talks.summary:
Gaelen Hadlett presents a privacy-focused computing curriculum for middle school students, developed through his New York City nonprofit. He argues that most computer science education, often funded by large technology companies, concentrates on coding and job preparation while leaving out how the internet is physically built, who controls it, and what data it exposes. The new material aims to combine computer science with social studies to fill that gap.

The curriculum explains digital infrastructure, from undersea cables and data centers to ISPs and payment apps, and walks through the laws and agencies that oversee it. Students read white papers, examine public data breaches, debate whether Edward Snowden was a hero or a traitor, and look at how school networks block websites. Practical lessons cover DNS blockers, VPNs and de-Googling phones, and a microbit-based cryptography extension is in testing. Hadlett shared a small survey of 16 students from a trial run, showing they knew little about the data collected on them yet felt capable of managing their privacy with the right tools.

Hadlett stressed that every lesson should end with something students can do, so they do not drift into a sense that privacy is already lost. Materials are planned for free release under Creative Commons, with online professional development for teachers. The takeaway for practitioners is a model for teaching privacy as civics, aligned with existing standards, that reaches students before high school.

talks.title: News From the 2600net IRC Network and Facebook Group
talks.teaser: Traces the 25-year history of the 2600net IRC network and its Facebook group, including attacks, legal pressure and lessons learned.
talks.summary:
This talk looks back over more than two decades of the 2600net IRC network and the 2600 Facebook group that grew alongside it. The speakers start with the network's origins after an earlier IRC service went offline, then explain how a volunteer team rebuilt it around a small set of standardized server software. A central rule adopted during the rebuild was that the operators must know everyone who runs infrastructure, after an unidentified host was removed from the network.

The middle of the talk covers the hard parts: DDoS attacks that kept the network down for long stretches, a rumored breach that turned out to be a joke about leaked old password hashes, trolls and long-lived botnets, and a failed attempt to introduce a warrant canary. The Facebook group was lost when its original admin died and his account was taken over through SMS verification, and the team later rebuilt it into a much larger group. The speakers also described a disinformation effort that used around 20,000 fake profiles and the way AI-generated spam started appearing in the group.

The closing part focuses on practices a small community can apply. The network keeps no logs beyond short diagnostic windows, expires inactive accounts after two years, encrypts data at rest, and keeps its attack surface small with a tightly limited set of exposed services. Plans for the future include adding Tor and I2P access, dual DNS, and better moderation for public channels. The main takeaway is that minimal data retention, least privilege and documented procedures help a volunteer network survive hostile conditions over the long term.

talks.title: Performance
talks.teaser: Presents a comedic set of rock songs and Game Boy chiptune music, with pizza-themed material and a tracker demo.
talks.summary:
Sam Mulligan opens by walking through the Game Boy's sound hardware and the Little Sound DJ tracker, showing how phrases are chained from top to bottom, how octaves and hops change a melody, and how the wave channel is run at double speed to make a kick and bass pattern sound fuller. The set then moves into a run of original songs with distorted guitar and Game Boy backing tracks. Topics include a search for Sasquatch, a time-travel tale, and a sing-along about being broke, with the audience joining in on call-and-response parts.

The middle of the set focuses on the pizza material behind an upcoming album of eight songs. These cover eating pizza every day, a delivery that never arrives, and a bad order that leads to a surreal, woozy mood. Mulligan also introduces the Dirty Wave M8 tracker, a newer device with eight channels, sample playback and FM synthesis, and uses it for a song about a weird pizza. Tempo changes and timing jokes recur as the performer adjusts the running order to fit the schedule.

There is no security technique to apply here. The practical lesson is how a small, constrained sound chip can be pushed into full arrangements through channel layering, timing offsets and tempo choices. The set is best read as a light, absurd live performance that rewards audience participation.

talks.title: Performance
talks.teaser: A live experimental sound performance blends structured improvisation with composed and interactive music.

talks.title: Hackers Got Talent
talks.teaser: Follows a HOPE talent show where attendees take the stage with everything from fire twirling to throat singing.
talks.summary:
The Hackers Got Talent show at HOPE 2024 invited attendees to sign up and perform any skill they liked, whether or not it related to hacking. Host Jason Scott opened by pulling reluctant audience members onto the stage and kept the proceedings moving through a long run of short acts.

The performances ranged widely: a stick twirler who used fire, a karaoke singer who deliberately sang an 80s power ballad badly, a throat singer demonstrating overtones on a live frequency analyzer, an ocarina player, someone imitating old telephone switching sounds, cartwheels, a tiny piano, dolphin noises, and a balloon inflated with the nose. A mix of panelists and audience members narrowed the field to five finalists, and a final round of applause chose the winner, a karaoke performer.

The evening closed with a prize, an Episode One jigsaw puzzle, and a note that demo scene films would screen in the same room afterward. The main takeaway is social rather than technical: the format rewards willingness to step up in front of a crowd, and it is a long-running piece of hacker culture at the conference.

talks.title: Closing Ceremonies
talks.teaser: Recaps how HOPE XV ran behind the scenes, from network and safety teams to volunteers, villages and thank-yous.
talks.summary:
The closing ceremony for HOPE XV at St John's University recaps how the weekend ran behind the scenes. Organizers and team leads take turns describing their areas, from networking and security to registration, the info desk, talks, workshops and villages. They also thank the volunteers, sponsors, partners and campus staff who made the event possible.

The network crew explains that they relied on the campus's existing wiring and a co-managed design, and that the connection was up within minutes of arrival. Because they were not in the main data path, they built a log analysis script to gauge usage, and they shared aggregate findings on peak throughput, client counts and common destinations. Other reports cover a joint safety arrangement between a first aid group, the security team and campus public safety, a check-in process that moved quickly, custom electronic badges, and a record number of workshops.

The final segment covers feedback that shaped changes, including food trucks, a reopened cafeteria and parking access, and it asks attendees to send further comments by email. Volunteers were offered shirts, and a cleanup was planned for that evening with no large teardown the next morning. The main message is that the event depended on many volunteers and partners, and that attendee input will guide the next gathering.
